findings.headline: £28m of LOBO loans repaid at par when lenders exercised rate-change options in May 2025; £18m remaining expected to trigger repayment in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The council held £51m of Lender Option Borrower Option loans at the start of 2025/26. Two LOBOs totalling £28m reached their lender option dates in May 2025; the lenders exercised their right to propose rate changes, and the council repaid these loans at par. The remaining £23m of LOBO borrowing includes £18m that will have lender option dates in 2026/27. The paper expects that with current interest rates elevated, lenders will again propose rate increases triggering further repayment at par and refinancing requirement.
findings.matters: This is a refinancing and liquidity event. As LOBOs are repaid at par, the council must secure replacement funding at current market rates (PWLB ~4.69%) versus original LOBO rates (3.81-4.35%), increasing debt service costs materially.
findings.figures: LOBOs repaid 2025/26: £28m at rates 3.81%-4.06%. Remaining LOBOs: £23m (£18m with 2026/27 option dates). Current PWLB rate c.4.69%. Existing LOBO rates range 3.81%-4.35%.
findings.quote: £18 million of the LOBO loans are subject to the lender having the right to change the rate of interest payable during 2026/27. With longer term interest rates remaining high, some or all of these loans are likely to be refinanced.

findings.headline: Major capital projects totalling £1.7bn of projected borrowing depend on income streams that 'may be delayed or will not materialise'.
findings.detail: The council's capital investment programme, particularly the arena funding strategy (£72m now, projected £180m by 2031), is structured as 'invest to save' and expected to be funded from future income. Section 51 explicitly warns: 'risks that the level of income, savings or capital receipts anticipated from such schemes will be delayed or will not materialise. This would have a detrimental long-term consequence on the Revenue budget and requires careful monitoring when considering future levels of additional borrowing.' This contingency risk directly affects the council's ability to service projected debt levels.
findings.matters: If material capital schemes do not generate projected income, the council will be unable to meet planned debt repayment schedules and will need to find further savings or increase council tax and rents, which is politically and operationally constrained.
findings.figures: Arena funding strategy: £72m (31 Mar 2026) projected to £180m (2030/31). Total CFR growth: £1,238m to £1,697m (2030/31). HRA financing costs: 29.70% of revenue.
findings.quote: risks that the level of income, savings or capital receipts anticipated from such schemes will be delayed or will not materialise. This would have a detrimental long-term consequence on the Revenue budget and requires careful monitoring when considering future levels of additional borrowing.

findings.headline: The council's short-term borrowing strategy depends on falling interest rates that forecasters now describe as 'increasingly uncertain'.
findings.detail: The council is taking predominantly short-term loans (1-7 years, average maturity 3.7 years) betting they can be refinanced at lower rates when they mature. However, the economic background notes that interest rate forecasts 'continue to be deferred and look increasingly uncertain'. The paper explicitly identifies key risks including rates 'not falling as quickly as forecasts suggest' or 'actually rising, resulting in unbudgeted interest costs for many years to come'. Section 58 warns this will result in 'a significant increase in short-term borrowing and refinancing risk' in 2026/27.
findings.matters: If interest rates do not fall as projected, the council will face materially higher costs when these loans mature, creating unanticipated budget pressure over multiple future years and reducing ability to fund services.
findings.figures: New PWLB average maturity: 3.7 years. New PWLB average rate: 4.69%. Long-dated rates ended year at four-year highs c.6.5%. Maturity profile shows 32.17% of borrowing due within 5 years.
findings.quote: Whilst economic forecasts remain that gilt yields and PWLB rates will fall across the whole curve over the next one to two years, the timing of such expectations continue to be deferred and look increasingly uncertain.

findings.headline: External borrowing increased by £168m to £1,148m and is projected to grow to £1.7bn by 2031.
findings.detail: External debt grew from £980m (31 March 2025) to £1,148m (31 March 2026), driven primarily by £231.8m of new PWLB borrowing taken in the year at an average rate of 4.69% and average maturity of only 3.7 years. The underlying Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) shows structural growth projected to reach £1,697m by 2030/31, reflecting major capital schemes including arena funding (£72m now, rising to £180m by 2031), affordable housing and 21st century schools programmes.
findings.matters: This structural increase in borrowing commits the council to long-term debt service costs and indicates ongoing refinancing needs, materially reducing future financial flexibility.
findings.figures: External debt: £1,148m (31 Mar 2026) vs £980m (31 Mar 2025). CFR: £1,238m actual vs £1,697m projected (2030/31). New PWLB funding: £231.8m at average 4.69% rate, 3.7 year average maturity.
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026, the Council had £1.148 billion of external borrowing. This was predominantly fixed interest rate borrowing from the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) payable on maturity.

findings.headline: Cash flow entry of £1.287 million has no supporting documentation; process review flagged as urgent for 2026-27
findings.detail: An entry recorded in the 'other financing activities' line of the cash flow statement (£1.287m) lacks documented support. The amount exceeds the audit's trivial reporting threshold (£0.88m). Auditors have flagged that the council must review its cash flow preparation process to ensure all entries are supported.
findings.matters: Lack of supporting evidence for material financing transactions indicates control weakness that affects the auditability and reliability of cash flow reporting
findings.figures: £1.287m unsupported, above trivial threshold of £0.88m
findings.quote: The Council have been unable to support the entry on the 'other financing activities' line (£1.287 million) in the cashflow statemen and as the untested balance is above trivial, we are required to bring this to your attention.

findings.headline: PPE indexation compliance gap: £1.53 million variance exceeds audit reporting threshold, requires 2026-27 process fix
findings.detail: Three assets were valued using professional valuation rather than CIPFA-mandated indexation in the first year of new requirements. The £1.53m variance exceeds the audit's trivial threshold (£0.87m) and remains uncorrected, but auditors require the council to ensure Code compliance going forward.
findings.matters: The council's process for implementing new CIPFA indexation requirements did not reliably achieve compliance on material items, signalling process gaps that could affect future statement accuracy
findings.figures: £1.53m variance, against trivial threshold of £0.87m
findings.quote: The difference between the professional and indexed valuation is immaterial (£1.53 million) in total for the three assets and no amendment has been requested however, as the difference is just above our trivial limit, we are required to bring this to your attention.

findings.headline: Multiple material misstatements identified in asset accounting, totaling over £22 million, all corrected before accounts issued
findings.detail: Auditors found three significant items: £9.2m omitted depreciation charge for newly acquired assets, £3.483m understatement of the Llanishen Fach building due to incorrect application of indexation, and £9.6m impairment reversal miscategorized as depreciation disposal. Management corrected all three before issuing the accounts.
findings.matters: Discovery of material errors in fixed asset accounting indicates control environment weaknesses that could affect future financial data reliability and lender confidence in reported asset values
findings.figures: £9.2m depreciation, £3.483m building valuation, £9.6m impairment (totaling over £22m)
findings.quote: The depreciation charge for newly acquired assets had been omitted.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure of £474.1 million approved with 47% funded by borrowing
findings.detail: The council spent £474.1 million on capital in 2025/26 including new schools, housing, the indoor arena and offices. Unsupported borrowing funded £95.8 million and invest-to-save borrowing funded £128.2 million. Much investment is assumed to pay for itself over future years from incidental income.
findings.matters: This investment increases the borrowing requirement when the council faces a £167 million budget gap and rising interest rates. The bet that incidental income will cover costs is hard to achieve.
findings.figures: £474.1 million capital expenditure; unsupported borrowing £95.766 million; invest-to-save borrowing £128.189 million
findings.quote: Significant capital expenditure investment is proposed in areas such as new schools; to address the condition of existing assets used in service delivery; to develop new council housing; for sustainable travel schemes; completion of the indoor arena and a replacement core office at Atlantic Wharf.

findings.headline: Section 151 Officer confirmed no emergency Section 114 notice was required
findings.detail: The council remained in a balanced budget position for 2025/26 through robust budget monitoring and management action. However, the officer notes the council is mindful of the risk of not being able to meet the balanced budget requirement in future years.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice signals financial distress and damages borrowing ability. Its absence is positive, but the officer's caveat about future years is a warning.

findings.detail: The council built up earmarked reserves during 2025/26 to improve financial resilience, though schools reserves declined. Reserves are being carefully prioritized to manage risks.
findings.matters: Higher reserves provide a buffer against unexpected costs and shortfalls, though they cannot solve a structural funding gap of £167 million.
findings.figures: Reserves increase not quantified in this section
findings.quote: The Council's overall level of earmarked reserves increased in the year to improve the Council's overall level of financial resilience.

findings.headline: Pension deficit improved by £50.8 million to £25.4 million
findings.detail: The Local Government Pension Scheme fund is now valued at 111% of future liabilities. The improvement came from strong investment performance relative to actuarial assumptions. The next valuation will not take place until 2028/29.
findings.matters: A well-funded pension scheme reduces contingent liabilities and frees up budget headroom. This is rare good news that eases pressure on the medium-term outlook.
findings.figures: Pension liability £25.360 million at 31 March 2026, decrease of £50.810 million from 2024/25; LGPS fund assets at 111% of liabilities
findings.quote: The Council's future liability in respect of pension benefits payable, compared to assets held, is £25.360 million at 31 March 2026. This is based on the latest actuarial assumptions, resulting in a decrease of £50.810 million from 2024/25

findings.headline: Housing emergency declared with new legislation in 2026 expected to increase demand further
findings.detail: Cabinet declared a housing emergency in December 2023 due to unprecedented demand for homelessness services and temporary accommodation. New homelessness legislation to be introduced in 2026 will lead to a further increase in demand on services. This is flagged as a red risk.

findings.quote: In December 2023, Cabinet declared a housing emergency in the city due to an unprecedented demand for homelessness services and Temporary Accommodation.

findings.headline: Growing number of deficit schools flagged as a red risk
findings.detail: Schools are facing financial shortfalls that could lead to cuts in staff and resources. The council notes that persistent deficits place additional pressures on the Local Authority funding position and pose a risk of irrecoverable debt.
findings.matters: Schools deficits create contingent liabilities for the council. The council cannot absorb school bailouts given the forward budget gap and constrained finances.
findings.figures: Number of deficit schools not quantified
findings.quote: Continued increase in the number of deficit schools. Schools facing financial shortfalls may struggle to maintain educational standards.

findings.headline: Collection rates fell for both council tax and non-domestic rates
findings.detail: Council tax collection rate dropped to 94.37% from 94.84%. Non-domestic rates collection fell to 93.89% from 95.72%. Both main revenue sources are being collected at lower rates than the prior year.
findings.matters: Lower collections reduce the revenue available to cover the budget, forcing either rate rises or cuts. This headwind comes exactly when the council faces a £167 million funding gap.
findings.figures: Council Tax collection 94.37% (2024/25: 94.84%); NDR collection 93.89% (2024/25: 95.72%)
findings.quote: The in-year collection rate was 94.37% (94.84% in 2024/25).

findings.headline: External borrowing increased by £167.6 million to £1.148 billion in one year
findings.detail: The council borrowed heavily to fund capital projects including new schools, housing, the indoor arena and offices. The Capital Financing Requirement is forecast to reach approximately £1.7 billion by the end of the medium-term plan.
findings.matters: This is major debt expansion at a time of rising interest rates. The cost of servicing this debt will absorb more of the revenue budget and compound difficulty closing the budget gap.
findings.figures: £167.619 million increase to £1.148 billion total; CFR forecast to approximately £1.7 billion
findings.quote: The net change in actual external borrowing during the year was an increase of £167.619 million to £1.148 billion.

findings.detail: The council faces a significant medium-term funding challenge where revenues will not keep pace with demand and inflation. The gap results from employee costs, price inflation, demand pressures in Adult Social Care, Looked After Children and Additional Learning Needs, and capital project costs.
findings.matters: This gap cannot be closed by efficiency alone and will force difficult choices about service levels or tax. A lender needs confidence the council can navigate this without defaulting.
findings.figures: £167 million budget gap between 2027/28 and 2030/31
findings.quote: Within the context of there being a Budget Gap of £167 million for the period 2027/28 to 2030/31.

findings.headline: The Port Health Authority's Annual Return was not approved by the 30 June regulatory deadline, breaching Regulation 15.
findings.detail: The auditor found that approval was not given before 30 June 2026, which meant Cardiff County Council as administering authority had not provided proper opportunity for electors' rights of inspection under the Public Audit (Wales) Act 2004. An addendum to the audit notice was published to notify electors of their rights over an unapproved Annual Return. The Committee is recommended to review arrangements to ensure future compliance.
findings.matters: Governance and audit compliance failures in bodies a council administers signal control environment weaknesses that lenders assess when deciding on credit.
findings.figures: 30 June 2026 deadline
findings.quote: Regulation 15 of the Accounts and Audit (Wales) Regs 2014 requires the Annual Return to be both properly certified by RFO and approved by the Chair of the Committee or Council meeting receiving the Return on or before 30 June.

findings.headline: Unqualified audit opinion with going concern confirmed for Cardiff Harbour Authority
findings.detail: The auditor intends to issue an unqualified opinion on the 2025-26 accounts. No material misstatements have been identified, no recommendations made, and going concern has been confirmed as the appropriate accounting basis. No material uncertainties have been identified regarding the authority's ability to continue operations for at least twelve months.
findings.matters: Lenders would want confirmation that the authority's accounts present a true and fair view, are free from material misstatement, and face no solvency or going concern issues that would threaten its ability to meet financial obligations.
findings.figures: Materiality set at £3.034 million (2% of gross assets). No uncorrected misstatements identified. No audit recommendations issued. Audit certification planned for 29 September 2026, ahead of the statutory 30 September deadline.
findings.quote: I have concluded that the use of the going concern basis of accounting in the preparation of the financial statements is appropriate. Based on the work I have performed, I have not identified any material uncertainties relating to events or conditions that, individually or collectively, may cast significant doubt on the Cardiff Harbour Authority's ability to continue to adopt the going concern basis of accounting

findings.headline: Cabinet-approved replacement ERP system (Finance, Procurement, HR, Payroll) to be implemented by autumn 2027.
findings.detail: The Council has procured a replacement enterprise resource planning system covering core financial and HR functions, with implementation planned for 2027/28. This is described as a significant programme of change; additional internal audit resources have been allocated.
findings.matters: ERP implementations carry high execution risk to financial controls and reporting; failure or delay could disrupt the Council's ability to close its budget gap.

findings.quote: Cabinet approval of the business case for a replacement Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system covering Finance, Procurement, HR and Payroll. This represents a significant programme of change

Control, Compliance, and embedding assurance actions were carried forward into the 2026/27 governance plan rather than closed, with no new governance issues identified requiring escalation.
findings.matters: Management restructures create risk to continuity of controls; carrying forward actions unresolved suggests the Council does not have confidence that its control environment meets acceptable standards.
findings.figures: No specific figures; 3 actions carried forward

findings.headline: Mandatory counter-fraud and corruption training achieved only 57% completion by end of March 2026; whistleblowing training at 39%.
findings.detail: The Council launched mandatory fraud awareness modules with a 100% completion target; by end of March 2026, average completion across the two modules was 57%. Whistleblowing training achieved only 39% of its target audience, described as having 'clear room for improvement'.
findings.matters: Low training compliance in fraud and whistleblowing indicates potential gaps in the control environment and a culture that may not support disclosure of concerns; this increases fraud risk.
findings.figures: 57% completion on counter-fraud training (target 100%); 39% on whistleblowing training (2,631 of target audience)

findings.headline: Sustained demand spikes in Social Care, Schools and Education, particularly Additional Learning Needs and specialist placements.
findings.detail: The Council explicitly noted demand-led pressures in high-cost service areas during the year. These pressures are cited as a driver of the medium-term financial challenge and have created an environment of sustained uncertainty.
findings.matters: Demand-led cost growth in these high-cost areas is a primary driver of the £167m budget gap; if demand continues to rise unchecked, the gap will widen and savings plans may not close it.

findings.quote: significant spikes in both demand for our services, not least in Social Care, Schools and Education particularly in respect to Additional Learning Needs and demand for Specialist placements

findings.detail: While 85% of audits were rated effective or effective with opportunity for improvement, the Council recorded two unsatisfactory audit opinions (both in schools/education) and four insufficient opinions requiring significant management action. Enhanced follow-up arrangements are in place.
findings.matters: Unsatisfactory audit opinions in education—a major cost area—indicate control weaknesses that may allow errors or overspending; a lender must understand whether these reflect isolated issues or systemic problems.
findings.figures: 85% effective or better; 2 unsatisfactory opinions; 4 insufficient opinions
findings.quote: Overall, 85% of audits were assessed as effective or effective with opportunity for improvement. Excluding audits carried forward from 2024/25, four audits were assessed as insufficient requiring significant management action and two audits received unsatisfactory opinions

findings.detail: The Governance and Audit Committee noted that while the Council's overall 2025/26 position was balanced, some particular directorates recorded significant overspends requiring control improvements. The Committee identified this as a sustained pressure requiring management attention.
findings.matters: Directorate overspends indicate loss of budget control in specific areas; a lender needs to understand which services are out of control and whether this pattern will recur.

findings.detail: While the Council delivered £10.923m in efficiency and income savings (88% of target), service change proposals delivered only £2.276m (76% of target). The statement notes that service change is more complex but that further such proposals will be required in future years.
findings.matters: Service change is the structural lever for closing budget gaps; poor delivery indicates difficulty managing the scale of change needed to close a £167m gap.
findings.figures: 88% efficiency savings (£10.923 million); 76% service change savings (£2.276 million)
findings.quote: The achievement of budget savings for 2025/26 was 88% for efficiency and income savings delivering £10.923 million  and 76 % for service change proposals delivering £2.276 million. Service Change proposals tend to be more complex and explain the lower achievable figure but it is likely that more service change savings proposals will be required in future years.

findings.matters: The scale and trajectory of the budget gap are the primary indicators of financial sustainability; a lender needs to see whether the council has credible plans to close it.

findings.quote: At 31 March 2026, the Council had £1.148 billion of external borrowing, with £234 million of new borrowing and £66.3 million of scheduled repayments during 2025/26.

findings.headline: Salary adjustment to Director level for interim Section 151 Officer: £104,326 to £152,392 per annum

The council notes the structural risk that permanent dual holding would compromise independent financial challenge and assurance, and references CIPFA expectation that the Section 151 Officer provides independent advice separate from the Chief Executive.

The Chief Finance and Deputy Section 151 Officer will hold the designation on an interim basis for up to 12 months while the Chief Executive reviews the senior management reporting structure. This interim arrangement creates a defined period of uncertainty about the permanent structure.
