The Local Government Pension Scheme fund's assets at 31 March 2025 covered 111% of estimated liabilities. The next formal triennial valuation will take place in 2028/29.
findings.matters: A well-funded pension scheme reduces the risk of emergency calls on council resources. This improvement demonstrates that at least one major long-term liability is being managed and is no longer a source of financial stress, freeing capacity for other priorities.
findings.figures: Pension liability decrease £50.810m; current liability £25.360m; fund at 111% of liabilities; next valuation 2028/29
findings.quote: This is based on the latest actuarial assumptions, resulting in a decrease of £50.810 million from 2024/25

findings.headline: Both Council Tax and non-domestic rates collection rates declined year-on-year in 2025/26.
findings.detail: Council Tax collection fell to 94.37% from 94.84% in 2024/25. Non-domestic rates collection fell to 93.89% from 95.72% in 2024/25. Council Tax income of £240.808m funds just over a quarter of the council's net expenditure; NDR contributes £137.400m after redistribution. Both declines represent revenue loss in a tight budget position.
findings.matters: Declining collection rates suggest economic stress among residents and businesses, and directly reduce the revenue available to the council. Each 0.5% fall in collection is material to a £250m+ income base.
findings.figures: Council Tax collection 94.37% (2024/25: 94.84%); NDR collection 93.89% (2024/25: 95.72%); Council Tax income £240.808m; NDR to council £137.400m
findings.quote: The in-year collection rate was 94.37% (94.84% in 2024/25).

findings.headline: Directorate budgets overspent by £2.090 million in 2025/26 despite overall containment, with significant adverse variances in children's and adult social care areas.
findings.detail: While the council contained overall spending within the £914.943m budget, directorate budgets recorded a net overspend of £2.090m. Economic Development overspent by £1.482m; Children's Services by £1.052m; Planning, Transport and Environment by £987k. Overspends in demand-led services (Children's, Adults) were offset by underspends elsewhere and capital financing variances. The paper notes final position improved as the year progressed with in-year efficiencies.
findings.matters: Overspends in services that cannot easily be reduced (children's and adults social care) indicate budget-setting may be insufficiently prudent. A lender would question whether future budgets adequately provision for these demand-led pressures.
findings.figures: Directorate overspend £2.090m; Children's Services £1.052m overspend; Economic Development £1.482m overspend; Planning, Transport & Environment £987k overspend
findings.quote: The directorate position reflected a net overspend of £2.090 million

findings.headline: Capital financing costs (interest and principal repayment) will increase significantly in future years as the capital programme matures.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that capital financing costs are to increase significantly in future years. Capital financing charges already include £34.6m in the Housing Revenue Account and are built into revenue budgets. As the Capital Financing Requirement grows toward £1.7bn, annual financing costs will grow materially, competing for revenue resources with service delivery.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether revenue budgets can absorb rising capital financing costs while maintaining service standards. If financing costs grow faster than income, the council's ability to repay debt or fund services deteriorates.
findings.figures: Capital financing in HRA £34.571 million; CFR forecast approximately £1.7 billion
findings.quote: The CFR and associated financing costs, interest and repayment, of capital investment are to increase significantly in future years

findings.headline: External borrowing increased by £167.6 million in a single year to £1.148 billion, with the Capital Financing Requirement forecast to reach approximately £1.7 billion.
findings.detail: Borrowing rose from £980.4m to £1.148bn in 2025/26. The council's Capital Financing Requirement is projected to reach approximately £1.7bn by the end of the medium-term plan. Capital spending of £474.1m was funded 47% from borrowing and invest-to-save schemes, compared to 39% from Welsh Government and other external grants. This borrowing funds new schools, housing, transport, and major projects including an indoor arena.
findings.matters: A lender tracks debt trajectory and affordability. At this rate, council debt could exceed £1.5bn within 2–3 years. The shift from grant-funded to borrowed capital represents a material change in the council's financing model and its future revenue obligations.
findings.figures: Borrowing increase £167.619 million; total external borrowing £1.148 billion; CFR forecast approximately £1.7 billion; capital spending £474.1m (20.2% unsupported borrowing, 27.04% invest-to-save borrowing)
findings.quote: The net change in actual external borrowing during the year was an increase of £167.619 million to £1.148 billion.

findings.headline: Cardiff faces a £167 million budget gap over 2027/28–2030/31, explicitly flagged as a critical red risk requiring fundamental change.
findings.detail: The council has identified a £167m shortfall between estimated funding and the cost of continuing services at current levels for the four-year period 2027/28–2030/31. This gap reflects funding failing to keep pace with demand, inflation, and service-specific pressures in Adult Social Care, Children's Services, and Additional Learning Needs. The Section 151 Officer states that future financial challenges cannot be met by efficiencies alone.
findings.matters: A lender must understand the council's plan to close a gap of this scale. If the plan relies on service cuts, asset sales, or future borrowing, each affects creditworthiness. The scale relative to annual spend (around 10% of budget) represents material risk to financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £167 million budget gap for period 2027/28 to 2030/31
findings.quote: Within the context of there being a Budget Gap of £167 million for the period 2027/28 to 2030/31.

findings.headline: Going concern assessment shows no material uncertainties affecting operational continuity
findings.detail: The auditor has concluded the going concern basis of accounting is appropriate and has not identified any material uncertainties that would cast doubt on the authority's ability to continue operations for at least twelve months.
findings.matters: Going concern issues are material concerns for lenders; absence of such uncertainties confirms the authority has no fundamental viability problems that would impair its ability to meet debt obligations.
findings.figures: No material uncertainties identified
findings.quote: Based on the work I have performed, I have not identified any material uncertainties relating to events or conditions that, individually or collectively, may cast significant doubt on the Cardiff Harbour Authority's ability to continue to adopt the going concern basis of accounting for a period of at least twelve months from when the financial statements are authorised for issue

findings.headline: Audit certification completed ahead of statutory 30 September deadline
findings.detail: The Wales Audit Office is certifying the accounts on 29 September 2026, one day before the statutory deadline. The audit has been substantially completed as set out in the June 2026 Audit Plan with no delays reported.
findings.matters: Early completion indicates no significant issues held up the audit and suggests effective financial management and timely accounting procedures at the authority.
findings.figures: 29 September 2026 certification date vs 30 September 2026 deadline
findings.quote: We are planning to certify your accounts on 29 September 2026, which is ahead of the deadline of 30 September 2026

findings.headline: Unqualified audit opinion issued with no material misstatements, significant findings, or audit recommendations
findings.detail: The Wales Audit Office intends to issue an unqualified opinion on Cardiff Harbour Authority's 2025-26 accounts. No uncorrected misstatements were identified during the audit, and no recommendations have been raised. Only one minor presentational amendment was requested to Note 6 on non-current asset measurement.
findings.matters: A clean audit with no recommendations confirms the council's financial statements are reliable, accounting records are accurate, and there are no control weaknesses or governance issues identified by auditors.
findings.figures: £3.034 million (gross assets)
findings.quote: We intend to issue an unqualified opinion on the accounts

findings.headline: Capital financing costs are rising across the MTFP while long-term borrowing rates exceed 6% and remain sticky
findings.detail: The council's medium-term financial plans show capital financing budgets increasing across the MTFP period. At the same time, UK interest rates for long-term borrowing remain above 6% and are not falling as quickly as previously anticipated. This combination of rising financing need and high rates increases the revenue budget burden of debt servicing.
findings.matters: Rising capital financing costs erode the revenue budget available for service delivery and increase the council's debt service burden; high rates also make any new borrowing more expensive.
findings.figures: Borrowing rates in excess of 6%, rates not falling at anticipated pace, capital financing budgets increasing into long term
findings.quote: The medium-term financial plans including the Arena Affordability model and Housing Revenue Account in particular, show the capital financing budgets increasing into the long term. UK Interest rates for long term borrowing are in excess of 6% and not falling as quickly as anticipated.

findings.headline: Real Living Wage rate—to be implemented May 2027—will not be announced until later in 2026, creating unquantified cost pressure
findings.detail: The council's budget assumes a particular Real Living Wage rate, but the actual rate will not be announced until later in 2026. If the announced rate exceeds the budgeted assumption, it will trigger direct pay pressure and increased cost of commissioned social care services with no time to adjust the budget.
findings.matters: A material unquantified upside cost pressure on statutory services occurring late in the budget year creates both planning and cash flow risk.
findings.figures: Implementation deadline May 2027, announcement timing not yet confirmed
findings.quote: Real Living Wage - rate to be implemented by May 2027 due for announcement later this year. If higher than planning assumptions, this will affect pay and price pressure, potential significant impact on commissioned care costs.

findings.headline: Useable reserves remain comparably low for an authority of Cardiff's size, despite a 2025/26 increase
findings.detail: While useable reserves did increase in 2025/26, benchmarking against authorities of similar size shows Cardiff's reserves remain below typical levels. This constrains the council's ability to absorb unexpected pressures or timing mismatches between spending and funding.
findings.matters: Low reserves relative to budget size reduce the buffer to absorb delivery failures, funding shortfalls, or demand shocks—increasing refinancing and borrowing risk.
findings.figures: Reserves described as 'comparably low for an authority of this size'
findings.quote: Identifies an increase in useable reserves in 2025/26. Informal benchmarking shows that Cardiff's useable reserves remain comparably low for an authority of this size.

findings.headline: No indicative Welsh Government funding figures for 2027/28; each 1% variance equals £7.2m, and only £4m resilience headroom available
findings.detail: The council is planning the 2027/28 budget on an assumption of 2% increase in Welsh Government funding (AEF), but has not received indicative figures. A 1% variance in settlement funding equates to approximately £7.2m. The council's Financial Resilience Mechanism provides capacity to absorb just over 0.5 percentage points of adverse settlement movement—meaning a shortfall beyond that requires additional action.
findings.matters: Planning certainty is essential to a lender. A funding gap that cannot be absorbed by existing resilience capacity or identified savings creates material repayment risk if settlement is less favourable than assumed.
findings.figures: 2% planning assumption, £7.2m per 1% variance, £4m Financial Resilience Mechanism, 0.5 percentage point absorption capacity
findings.quote: No indicative funding figures for 2027/28 and beyond. Planning assumptions reflect a 2% increase. In cash terms, each 1% difference in AEF equates to c£7.2m – absence of indicatives presents key risk to planning... A degree of resilience to less favourable settlement is available via the Council's £4m Financial Resilience Mechanism (FRM) Budget – capacity to cope with an adverse fluctuation of just over 0.5 percentage points on current funding assumptions.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account shows budget gap of £1.576m in 2027/28 and £10.62m over MTFP, to be funded from reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The HRA projects a budget gap of £1.576m in 2027/28 and £10.62m over the MTFP period, even after assuming £4.16m in efficiency savings and service change. The council intends to manage this gap by drawing on HRA earmarked reserves. A detailed five-year efficiencies plan is to be developed.
findings.matters: HRA reserve depletion limits headroom for future rental decisions and capital investment in social housing stock, and signals that operating deficits are structural.
findings.figures: £1.576 million 2027/28 gap, £10.62 million over MTFP period, £4.16 million assumed savings
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget and MTFP indicated a temporary budget gap for the HRA, estimated at £1.576 million for 2027/28 and £10.62 million over the MTFP period, after assuming targeted efficiency savings and service change estimated at £4.16 million. The budget gap will require use of the available HRA earmarked reserves in the medium term.

findings.headline: Adult social care care-home recommissioning will cost up to £4.0m more in 2027/28, with commitment locked in before inflation is finalised
findings.detail: The council is recommissioning older people's care home placements under a new framework approach. The estimated additional cost is £4.0m in 2027/28 (plus £0.2m in 2028/29). To meet implementation timescales, rates must be committed to by May 2027, but will not be adjusted for estimated 2027/28 inflation until disclosure to providers—creating a timing mismatch that locks in costs before all variables are known.
findings.matters: A £4m unfunded pressure on a statutory service signals budget failure; the commitment being made before inflation is finalised represents both a planning risk and a cash flow timing risk.
findings.figures: £4.0 million in 2027/28, £0.200 million in 2028/29, £1.4m estimated inflation impact
findings.quote: To note the pressures and timescales associated with the recommissioning of Care Home Placements for Older People and to agree to the inclusion within the Council's Budget of the estimated additional costs of up to a maximum of £4.0 million in 2027/28 (being the impact of estimated framework rates plus inflation), and £0.200 million in 2028/29.

findings.headline: £163.7m budget gap over MTFP period requires £118.9m in savings, but the council achieved only 85% of savings target in 2025/26
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Plan shows pressures of £223.7m 2027/28–2030/31, leaving a budget gap of £163.7m after funding and council tax. The strategy relies on £118.9m of savings over the four years. However, the council achieved only 85% of planned savings in 2025/26, raising delivery risk on the more ambitious targets now required.
findings.matters: A lender assessing repayment capacity needs confidence a council can deliver promised savings; a record of 85% achievement makes £118.9m of planned cuts material delivery risk.
findings.figures: £163.7m total budget gap, £223.7m pressures, £118.9m savings required, 85% achievement rate 2025/26
findings.quote: Total Budget Gap 45.0 35.4 37.6 45.7 163.7... Savings (34.6) (24.5) (26.1) (33.7) (118.9)... The percentage of savings achieved was 85% for 2025/26.

findings.headline: Audit completion pending assurances from subsidiary company auditors; group consolidation not finalized
findings.detail: Outstanding queries remain and auditors are awaiting assurances from the auditors of SEW CJC and the council's consolidated subsidiaries Cardiff City Transport Ltd and Cardiff Heat Network Ltd. Final audit review processes have not been completed at the time of this report.
findings.matters: Outstanding group audit work means the final unqualified opinion is conditional on subsidiary assurances; delayed completion could affect financial reporting timeliness.
findings.figures: Certification planned 29 September 2026
findings.quote: There are a number of queries that remain outstanding at the time of writing; we are pending the receipt of the requested assurances from the auditors of the SEW CJC and the auditors of the Council's consolidated subsidiaries – Cardiff City Transport Ltd and Cardiff Heat Network Ltd.

findings.headline: Cash flow statement contains £1.287m unsupported entry indicating process control weakness
findings.detail: The council could not provide supporting documentation for a £1.287m entry on the 'other financing activities' line in the cash flow statement. The balance remained untested and exceeded the auditors' trivial threshold, requiring them to flag a material weakness in the cash flow preparation process.
findings.matters: An unsupported material entry in cash flow reporting indicates weakness in liquidity management controls; cash flow integrity is critical for lenders assessing the council's ability to meet obligations.
findings.figures: £1.287m unsupported on 'other financing activities' line
findings.quote: The Council have been unable to support the entry on the 'other financing activities' line (£1.287 million) in the cashflow statemen and as the untested balance is above trivial, we are required to bring this to your attention. Going forward for 2026-27 the Council needs to review its process for preparing the cash-flow statement and ensure all entries are fully supported.

findings.headline: Asset revaluation process fails to comply with new 2025-26 CIPFA code requirement for indexation
findings.detail: CIPFA introduced new mandatory indexation requirements for asset revaluation in 2025-26. The council used full professional valuation for three assets where the code requires indexation, creating a £1.53m difference between approaches. While immaterial, the auditors identified a code compliance failure that must be corrected in 2026-27.
findings.matters: Non-compliance with mandatory accounting standards indicates the finance function did not fully understand new requirements, representing an implementation risk for future years.
findings.figures: £1.53m difference between professional and indexed valuations across three assets
findings.quote: Having reviewed the rationale for the three valuations, we are of the view that indexation should have been applied to these assets, in accordance with the CIPFA Code guidance. Going forward for 2026-27 and future years, the Council needs to ensure that it is Code compliant in this area.

findings.headline: Major audit corrections required: £9.2m depreciation charge entirely omitted, £3.483m building valuation error
findings.detail: The audit identified material accounting errors that management corrected: £9.2m depreciation charge on newly acquired assets was entirely omitted; £3.483m understatement of the Llanishen Fach building which had been omitted from revaluation; £4.630m understatement of non-domestic rates collectible; and £9.6m impairment reversal misclassified as depreciation.
findings.matters: Corrections of this magnitude indicate control weaknesses in fixed asset management and revenue recognition; while caught by audit, they represent control failures that lenders would expect the council to remediate.
findings.figures: £9.2m depreciation omission; £3.483m building understatement; £4.630m NDR understatement; £9.6m impairment misclassification; £1.378m contribution to CSCJES unreported
findings.quote: During our audit, we identified misstatements that have been corrected by management, but which we consider should be drawn to your attention.

findings.headline: Cabinet approved a major Enterprise Resource Planning system replacement covering Finance, Procurement, HR and Payroll, with implementation planned for 2027/28.
findings.detail: The Council approved a business case for replacement ERP systems covering Finance, Procurement, HR and Payroll. Procurement concluded in March 2026 with a successful bidder selected. Detailed implementation planning is scheduled for early 2026/27 with system delivery during 2027/28 (approximately 18 months from late 2026). Additional internal audit resources have been allocated to provide real-time assurance. The Committee has flagged the need for regular reporting on progress and risk management given programme scale and complexity.
findings.matters: A major core systems replacement is both an opportunity and a risk. Successful implementation could deliver improved financial controls and efficiency; failure could impact financial reporting quality and control during a period when the council is managing a £167m budget gap and significant demand growth. Implementation timing during acute financial pressure adds execution risk.
findings.figures: 18-month implementation window, delivery during 2027/28
findings.quote: Cabinet approval of the business case for a replacement Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system covering Finance, Procurement, HR and Payroll. This represents a significant programme of change.

findings.headline: The Public Services Ombudsman for Wales issued a Public Interest Report on failures in the Responsive Repairs Service.
findings.detail: The Governance and Audit Committee considered a Public Interest Report from the Ombudsman concerning failures in the Responsive Repairs Service. Improvement activity was already underway including a comprehensive service review and Repairs Improvement Project under appropriate oversight. The Committee has committed to seeking assurance from scrutiny, internal audit, and senior officers that governance and control have been appropriately addressed.
findings.matters: A Public Interest Report represents a serious governance and service delivery failure that has triggered an ombudsman investigation. Responsive repairs typically serve vulnerable older people and disabled residents. The failure signals control gaps in service delivery and residual reputational and governance risk until remediation is demonstrated.
findings.figures: None specified in relation to the scale of failure
findings.quote: The Committee has considered a Public Interest Report issued by the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales concerning failures in the Responsive Repairs Service.

findings.headline: Mandatory training compliance fell short of target at 83% actual against 85% target; fraud awareness training achieved only 57%.
findings.detail: Across all mandatory training modules (corporate safeguarding, data protection, fraud awareness, equality training and others), the council achieved 83% compliance against an 85% target. Separately, the two new Counter-Fraud, Bribery and Corruption training modules introduced in 2025/26 achieved only 57% take-up (4,061 staff completing against a target audience). The Chief Executive noted that not all mandatory modules are at 100% and stated there will be a review to prioritise fundamental compliance and cultural training.
findings.matters: Substandard mandatory training compliance, especially for fraud awareness, represents a material control risk. Low fraud awareness completion (57%) during a period of significant budget pressure and demand surge signals that frontline staff may lack awareness of fraud policies and procedures when financial discipline and probity are most critical.
findings.figures: 83% vs 85% target across all mandatory modules; 57% take-up of fraud training (4,061 staff)
findings.quote: By the end of March 2026, an average of 4,061 staff have completed each training module but the take up is 57% and requires further work

findings.headline: Two internal audit reports received unsatisfactory opinions in 2025/26; both related to schools and education settings.
findings.detail: Of completed audits, two received unsatisfactory opinions and four were assessed as insufficient requiring significant management action. Both unsatisfactory opinions related to schools or education. The Governance and Audit Committee noted delays in implementing school audit recommendations and raised concerns over the governance of school balances and contracting arrangements. Enhanced school management arrangements are being delivered but the Committee will keep the area under close observation.
findings.matters: Unsatisfactory audit opinions represent significant control weaknesses. Schools governance carries both financial and reputational risk for councils. The number of outstanding audit recommendations in education and delays in implementation indicate governance gaps in a sector handling public funds and serving vulnerable children.
findings.figures: 2 unsatisfactory audit opinions; 4 insufficient audits; 85% of audits rated effective or effective with opportunity for improvement
findings.quote: The two internal audit assurance reports with unsatisfactory opinions in 2025/26 related to schools / education settings.

findings.headline: Some directorates had significant overspends in 2025/26 requiring control improvements despite the overall budget being balanced.
findings.detail: The Governance and Audit Committee noted that whilst the overall council position was balanced, specific directorates recorded significant overspends. The Committee stated that management attention and control improvements are required in these directorates to achieve budget savings proposals. This indicates mid-year control failures in budget monitoring or spending management at directorate level, particularly concerning given sustained financial pressure.
findings.matters: Directorate-level overspends despite overall balance signal control weaknesses in budget stewardship and spending management. For a lender, this indicates governance gaps in how the council monitors and manages spending at operational level, a concern during a period when financial discipline is critical.
findings.figures: Unquantified directorate overspends within balanced overall position
findings.quote: whilst the overall financial position was balanced, some particular directorates had significant overspends for which control improvements are needed

findings.headline: The council has identified a medium-term budget gap of £167.1 million for 2027/28 to 2030/31.
findings.detail: The Council's final refresh of Medium-Term Financial Plan assumptions in the 2026/27 budget report identified a budget gap of £167.1 million across four years. This reflects sustained financial pressures from funding constraints, inflationary costs exceeding funding increases, and significant demand growth particularly in social services and education (notably Additional Learning Needs and specialist placements). The Governance and Audit Committee identified financial resilience as a priority area for 2026/27 monitoring.
findings.matters: A lender would view this as the critical metric of financial sustainability. At £167.1 million over four years, the gap represents a substantial structural challenge that will require major service redesign, significant tax increases, or both. This is beyond routine budget management and signals multi-year financial stress.
findings.figures: £167.1 million gap for 2027/28 to 2030/31
findings.quote: identified a medium-term gap for 2027/28 to 2030/31 of £167.1 million

findings.headline: Service change savings delivered only 76% of target in 2025/26 against 88% for efficiency savings, highlighting execution risk on more complex proposals.
findings.detail: The Council's budget savings tracking shows divergent performance between proposal types. Efficiency and income savings achieved 88% of target (£10.923 million delivered), while service change proposals delivered only 76% of target (£2.276 million). The paper acknowledges that service change proposals are more complex, but with a £167.1 million budget gap ahead over four years, this shortfall signals potential execution risk on the scaled-up savings required.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's ability to close a £167m budget gap needs to understand delivery track record on complex savings. Service change proposals tend to be larger and more transformational, so 76% delivery matters materially for the council's financial resilience.
findings.figures: 88% efficiency savings (£10.923 million); 76% service change (£2.276 million)
findings.quote: The achievement of budget savings for 2025/26 was 88% for efficiency and income savings delivering £10.923 million  and 76 % for service change proposals delivering £2.276 million.

findings.headline: Treasury management team is under resource pressure managing an increasingly complex £1.1bn borrowing programme
findings.detail: The council identifies that "the requirements to meet high standards, accuracy and governance requirements are significant for a small specialist team." It acknowledges need to allocate additional resources and use external services to support short and long-term tactical borrowing decisions. This matters because the council is pursuing a sophisticated strategy of short-term borrowing and refinancing that requires precise execution.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that the council has adequate capacity to execute a complex refinancing strategy without operational error. Understaffing in treasury function during a period of rising volumes and complexity increases execution risk.
findings.figures: External debt £1.148 billion; no specific staffing figures disclosed
findings.quote: The requirements to meet high standards, accuracy and governance requirements are significant for a small specialist team.

findings.headline: Council is internally borrowing at near-maximum levels, forcing shift to external borrowing just as rates remain elevated
findings.detail: Cardiff holds £90m of internal borrowing (temporary cash balances used instead of external borrowing) against a targeted maximum of £100m, up from £80m in the prior year. The strategy document explicitly warns that "deferring borrowing is only a short-term measure and could expose the Council to higher borrowing rates and costs in the future." As internal cash declines (average daily balance £114.7m but year-end investments only £67.9m), the council will be forced to increase external borrowing.
findings.matters: The council's internal borrowing capacity is nearly exhausted at a point when external rates are at four-year highs. This timing risk is material to future debt servicing costs.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing £90m (targeted level circa £100m); average daily cash balance £114.7m; year-end investments £67.9m
findings.quote: However deferring borrowing is only a short-term measure and could expose the Council to higher borrowing rates and costs in the future.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing substantially with housing revenue account financing costs now consuming 30% of rents
findings.detail: The council's underlying borrowing need (CFR) grew from £1.060bn at 1 April 2025 to £1.238bn at 31 March 2026 and is forecast to grow to £1.697bn by 2030/31. The ratio of capital financing costs to revenue is rising materially: HRA gross capital financing ratio is 29.70% at 2025/26 actual, rising to 37.48% by 2030/31. This growth is driven by major capital commitments assumed to generate future income or savings, including the indoor arena, new affordable housing, and school replacement programme.
findings.matters: The rising CFR and financing cost ratios constrain the council's financial flexibility and raise questions about whether major schemes will generate the income and savings assumed. The HRA ratio of nearly 30% leaves limited room for shocks.
findings.figures: CFR £1.060bn (Apr 2025) to £1.238bn (Mar 2026) to £1.697bn (2030/31); HRA gross financing ratio 29.70% (2025/26 actual) rising to 37.48% (2030/31); GF gross financing ratio 6.76% rising to 8.47%
findings.quote: An increasing ratio limits the scope for additional borrowing in future years and reduces the Council's overall flexibility when making decisions on the allocation of its revenue resources.

findings.headline: Interest rate forecasts have repeatedly been deferred and market reality is diverging from council's strategy
findings.detail: The council's entire borrowing strategy depends on the forecast that PWLB rates will fall over the next one to two years. However, the paper notes explicitly that "the timing of such expectations continue to be deferred and look increasingly uncertain." Gilt yields rose materially in March 2026, reversing falls earlier in the year. The council also lists as a specific risk: "Interest rates actually rising, resulting in unbudgeted interest costs for many years to come, when expenditure on projects has already been undertaken."
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that the council's strategy is resilient to the actual economic scenarios that are most likely. The council's own risk assessment identifies rising rates as a material possibility.
findings.figures: PWLB rates c6.5%; rates described as four-year highs
findings.quote: Whilst economic forecasts remain that gilt yields and PWLB rates will fall across the whole curve over the next one to two years, the timing of such expectations continue to be deferred and look increasingly uncertain.

findings.headline: Council's short-term borrowing strategy assumes interest rates will fall but PWLB rates are at four-year highs
findings.detail: Cardiff borrowed £231.8m from PWLB during 2025/26 at an average rate of 4.69% and average maturity of 3.7 years, on the assumption that interest rates would fall and these loans could be refinanced at lower rates when they mature. However, PWLB rates ended the year around 6.5% (four-year highs), and the council notes that "reductions assumed as part of economic forecasts have not yet materialised" and the timing of expected falls "continue to be deferred and look increasingly uncertain."
findings.matters: If interest rates do not fall as assumed, the council will face material unbudgeted interest costs for many years on the full value of expenditure already undertaken, and will have a large portfolio of loans maturing in narrow time windows requiring refinancing simultaneously.
findings.figures: £231.8m new PWLB borrowing at average rate 4.69%, average maturity 3.7 years; PWLB rates at c6.5%
findings.quote: Given the current forecasts that interest rates will fall, any loans taken to meet the borrowing requirement are short term loans 1-7 years. Whilst this may have higher short term costs of interest, it is assumed they can be refinanced at lower interest rates when they mature.

findings.headline: £18 million of LOBO loans face lender refinancing option during 2026/27
findings.detail: Cardiff held six LOBO loans totalling £51m at the start of 2025/26. It repaid £28m during the year. Of the remaining £23m, £18m are subject to the lender's right to change the rate of interest during 2026/27, at which point the council must either accept the new rate or repay at par. The council notes these loans "are likely to be refinanced" given current interest rate levels.
findings.matters: The council faces a material refinancing need in 2026/27 that could result in significantly higher interest costs if lenders exercise their call options.
findings.figures: £51m LOBO portfolio at start of year; £28m repaid during year; £18m at call in 2026/27
findings.quote: Of the remaining £23 million, £18 million of the LOBO loans are subject to the lender having the right to change the rate of interest payable during 2026/27. The Council has the right to refuse the change, triggering early repayment and the need to re-finance. These loans have been in place for some years and with longer term interest rates remaining high, some or all of these loans are likely to be refinanced.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Appendix 3 Financial Resilience Snapshot
findings.headline: Long-term borrowing ratio rises to 90% of revenue funding, from 83% the prior year
findings.detail: The ratio of long-term borrowing to available tax and grant funding has increased significantly year-on-year from 83% to 90%. Capital financing requirement as a percentage of net revenue budget has also risen from 97% to 105%, indicating debt service is consuming an increasing share of annual revenue.
findings.matters: Rising borrowing ratios indicate the council's debt burden is growing relative to its annual revenue funding, which constrains fiscal flexibility and indicates increasing reliance on borrowing to fund capital investment.
findings.figures: LT Borrowing to Tax & AEF rises from 83% (2024/25) to 90% (2025/26); Capital Funding Req/Net Revenue rises from 97% to 105%
findings.quote: LT Borrowing to Tax & AEF 96% 94% 86% 83% 90%

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Appendix 3 Financial Resilience Snapshot
findings.headline: General contingency reserve exhausted; earmarked reserves declining from £177m to £148m
findings.detail: The council's general contingency reserve has been depleted to zero and will remain at zero through 2025/26. Overall useable earmarked reserves are forecast to decline from £177m at March 2026 to £148m at March 2027, representing a 16% reduction in fiscal buffers over one year.
findings.matters: Declining reserves and exhaustion of contingency buffers reduce the council's ability to manage unexpected pressures or timing variations, increasing financial fragility.
findings.figures: General contingency at £0; earmarked reserves decline from £177m (March 2026) to £148m (March 2027)
findings.quote: General Contingency 3,000 2,000 1,000 0 0

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Appendix 3 Financial Resilience Snapshot
findings.headline: Four-year budget gap of £292m maximum, £27m minimum, with base case £167m
findings.detail: The medium-term financial plan identifies a budget gap requiring closure through savings or other intervention. The base case assumes £167m of gap over four years, but scenario analysis shows it could fall to £27m in optimistic conditions or rise to £292m if economic stress and other adverse scenarios materialize.
findings.matters: A budget gap of this scale (base case represents roughly 17% of annual budget) requires credible plans to close it. A lender would need to understand how this gap is being managed and whether plans are realistic.
findings.figures: Base case £167m; scenario range £27m–£292m over medium term
findings.quote: Maximum budget gap over medium term period is £292m, minimum is £27m and the average was £160m which is in line with the base case of £167m.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Appendix 3 Financial Resilience Snapshot
findings.headline: Adult social care now represents almost 20% of the council's budget and faces demographic pressures to 2035
findings.detail: Adult social care spending has grown 66% in cash terms since 2020/21, significantly outpacing the overall council budget growth of 47%. The service now represents almost one-fifth of total council spending. The council identifies a significant projected increase in the over-65 population through 2035 that will drive further demand.
findings.matters: This represents a structural budget risk: a service representing one-fifth of spend is growing faster than overall resources, with demographic trends indicating demand will accelerate for the next decade.
findings.figures: Adult services budget growth of 66% since 2020/21; overall council budget growth of 47%; now 20% of total budget
findings.quote: Adult Social Care's net budget has increase by 66% in cash terms since 2020/21 compared to the overall Councils net budget increase of 47%. It now represents almost 20% of the total. A significant increase in the over 65 population is projected to 2035, which will increase demand on services.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Appendix 3 Financial Resilience Snapshot
findings.headline: Children's services external residential placements rising 31% in volume while costs per placement rise 57%
findings.detail: The number of external residential placements has grown from 2021/22 baseline while the council has shifted away from cheaper fostering toward more expensive residential care. Average placement costs are rising faster than volume, and the cost differential between residential and fostering has widened from 389% to 491%.
findings.matters: This represents dual cost pressure: volume growth plus unit cost inflation in a service area, with the mix shifting toward the most expensive options, driving future budget pressures.
findings.figures: External residential places +31%, average costs +57%, cost premium expands from 389% to 491%
findings.quote: The number of external residential places since 2021/22 has increased by 31%, while average costs have increased by 57%.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Appendix 3 Financial Resilience Snapshot
findings.headline: Additional learning needs budgets have grown 95% in five years, twice the council's overall budget growth rate
findings.detail: ALN-related budgets in the education directorate have grown significantly faster than the council's overall budget, reflecting both increased demand for specialist placements and rising costs in the independent sector. This growth rate outpaces the council's ability to fund it from overall budget growth.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender would recognize this as a structural budget pressure requiring action; demand growth is outpacing overall budget growth by a factor of two.
findings.figures: 95% growth over 5 years in ALN budgets versus approximately 47% growth in overall council budget
findings.quote: Budgets associated with ALN have grown by 95% in the last 5 years, twice the rate of the overall Council's net budget

findings.headline: 58 compensation events totalling £8.6m signal ongoing contract management and cost growth risks
findings.detail: The NEC contract accommodates compensation events for unforeseen changes. Fifty-eight have been implemented, adding £8.6m to the contract value. Principal drivers are environmental approval delays (£2.6m), rock armour design changes from unsuitable ground conditions (£5.5m after value engineering), and a revised piling solution (£1m). The scale and frequency indicate material project risks continue to materialize.
findings.matters: Frequent compensation events signal that project risks are not fully contained and further cost pressures may emerge; they indicate active cost growth despite the contract framework, suggesting governance or risk management challenges.
findings.figures: 58 compensation events; £8,640,880 total; environmental delay £2.6m; rock armour redesign £5.5m; piling £1m
findings.quote: To date, 58 compensation events have been implemented through the NEC contract, adding £8,640,880 to the original contract award value.

findings.headline: Completion date extended by 285 days to August 2027; environmental approval delays accounted for 270 days
findings.detail: Original completion was scheduled for 31 October 2026; the scheme now extends to 12 August 2027. Environmental approvals from Natural Resources Wales caused 270 of the 285-day delay. The council was forced to award the contract before approvals were in place to secure Welsh Government funding. The extended timeline keeps capital tied up longer and leaves the council exposed to further cost pressures.
findings.matters: The 10-month programme delay extends the council's cost exposure and capital commitment; further cost pressures may emerge during the extended delivery; the delay reflects governance challenges in securing multi-agency environmental approval.
findings.figures: Original completion 31 October 2026; new completion 12 August 2027; extension 285 days; environmental delays 270 days
findings.quote: The construction contract commenced on 9 October 2023 with an original completion date of 31 October 2026. The current programme position extends completion to 12 August 2027, representing an extension of 285 days.

findings.headline: Welsh Government will not fund cost overruns; council will service 25-year debt for entire overspend
findings.detail: Welsh Government's £30.5m contribution is not a cash grant but reimbursement of borrowing costs over 25 years. The council requested additional grant funding for the £9.5m overspend, but Welsh Government declined as the Coastal Flood Programme has ended. The council must finance the entire overspend through borrowing and service the debt for 25 years.
findings.matters: The council's long-term debt service liability is substantially larger than initially planned; lenders must assess whether the council can service the extended commitment without squeezing other priorities.
findings.figures: Welsh Government reimbursement £30,546,614 (fixed); overspend not funded £9,540,979; repayment period 25 years
findings.quote: It should be noted that the Welsh Government funding approach is not a cash grant towards the expenditure, but to re-imburse the Council for the costs of servicing borrowing which would need to be taken by the Council, over a period of twenty-five years. Welsh Government have indicated they are not able to contribute towards additional costs.

findings.headline: Capital scheme overspent by £9.5m (26%), with council contribution increasing from £5.4m to £14.9m
findings.detail: The original approved budget was £35.9m (85% Welsh Government, 15% Council). The June 2026 forecast is £45.5m. Welsh Government's £30.5m contribution remains fixed; the council's share rises to £14.9m, a 177% increase. The council approved £10m additional borrowing in March 2026 but cost growth may exceed this.
findings.matters: A 26% overspend on a major project indicates delivery challenges; the council's increased debt burden will persist for 25 years; further cost pressures could exhaust the approved £10m additional borrowing facility.
findings.figures: £35,937,193 → £45,478,172; Council contribution £5,390,579 → £14,931,558; additional borrowing £10m
findings.quote: As of June 2026, the forecast total scheme cost is £45,478,172, an increase of £9,540,979. Welsh Government funding remains fixed at £30,546,614, while the forecast Cardiff Council capital programme contribution rises to £14,931,558.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Care Home Framework Appendix E - Risks and Mitigation
findings.headline: Care home ownership changes over 8-year framework term cannot be novated and create temporary capacity gaps
findings.detail: The council identifies a RED pre-mitigation risk that care home sales and ownership changes will result in temporary loss of approved provider status and potential capacity gaps if reapplication is delayed. Contracts cannot be simply novated due to procurement and legal constraints. Mitigations include change-of-control clauses and interim payment arrangements; post-mitigation risk is Amber.
findings.matters: Unexpected loss of framework providers during the 8-year term will force emergency spot-purchasing at higher rates and create service disruption.
findings.figures: Framework lifetime: up to 8 years
findings.quote: During the lifetime of the framework (up to 8 years), care homes may be sold or change ownership. Due to procurement and legal constraints: contracts cannot simply be novated to a new legal entity

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Care Home Framework Appendix E - Risks and Mitigation
findings.headline: Fixed pricing model may not respond quickly enough to inflation and workforce costs, risking provider exit and market instability
findings.detail: The council identifies a RED pre-mitigation risk that fixed pricing will not respond quickly to market pressures (inflation, workforce costs), potentially leading to reduced provider participation, increased off-framework placements, and financial instability. Mitigations include regular pricing review mechanisms, annual uplifts, enhanced payments for complexity, and provider financial monitoring.
findings.matters: If providers exit the framework due to inadequate fees, the council loses the cost-containment benefit of fixed pricing and must use spot-purchasing, multiplying cost exposure.
findings.figures: Red pre-mitigation risk; annual fee review mechanism required
findings.quote: The fixed pricing model may not respond quickly to market pressures (e.g. inflation, workforce costs), potentially leading to: reduced provider participation, increased off-framework placements, financial instability in the market

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Care Home Framework Appendix E - Risks and Mitigation
findings.headline: Rising demand for complex dementia care may drive cost pressures beyond framework design capacity
findings.detail: The council identifies a RED pre-mitigation risk that demand growth, particularly for complex dementia care, will outpace the framework design and create cost pressures. This is separate from capacity shortages—it is about demand escalation itself. Post-mitigation is Amber/Green through demand reviews and integration with community alternatives.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled demand growth for higher-cost care categories will force either unbudgeted spending or service rationing and delayed placements.
findings.figures: Pre-mitigation risk: Red; post-mitigation: Amber/Green
findings.quote: Rising demand, particularly for complex dementia care, may outpace the design of the framework, leading to: cost pressures

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Care Home Framework Appendix E - Risks and Mitigation
findings.headline: Significant capacity shortages in care home market (35% no bids; 39% for dementia) mean framework-first model is at risk
findings.detail: Evidence of existing shortage shows 35% of placement bids overall and 39% for dementia nursing receive no offers. The council risks demand outstripping supply, particularly for dementia and complex care, leading to delays in hospital discharge and forced reliance on expensive off-framework spot-purchasing. Mitigations include targeted fee uplifts for high-acuity care and workforce development.
findings.matters: If the new framework cannot meet demand due to inadequate capacity, the council will be forced to purchase at higher spot-market rates, creating unbudgeted expenditure despite fixed framework pricing.
findings.figures: 35% no bids overall; 39% for dementia nursing
findings.quote: Evidence shows significant difficulty sourcing placements (e.g. 35% no bids overall; 39% for dementia nursing).

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Care Home Framework Appendix E - Risks and Mitigation
findings.headline: Council faces RED risk that placement costs will exceed budget due to market pressures and expensive spot-purchasing
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies a RED pre-mitigation risk that placement costs will increase due to market pressures, fee variation, and reliance on high-cost purchasing arrangements, resulting in financial pressures. Post-mitigation, this falls to Amber/Green through fixed framework rates, framework-first approach, controlled enhancements, and annual fee reviews.
findings.matters: This is an explicit recognition of unbudgeted expenditure risk in a major service area; if spot-purchasing occurs at scale, it will create a material cost overrun.
findings.figures: Pre-mitigation risk: Red; post-mitigation: Amber/Green
findings.quote: There is a risk that placement costs increase due to market pressures, fee variation, and reliance on high-cost purchasing arrangements, resulting in financial pressures for the Council.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Annual Wellbeing Report Appendix 3a Performance Panel Letter, Recommendations and Observations
findings.headline: Pattern of capital project delays across transport and flood defence schemes; council has strengthened project management capacity.
findings.detail: Scrutiny identified a pattern of delays in major capital projects across transport and flood defence, arising from complexity factors including funding issues and road management constraints. The council has responded by putting in place strengthened project management capacity. Scrutiny recommended that project timescales be set more realistically.
findings.matters: A pattern of capital project delays indicates historic execution and planning weakness; while management improvements have been made, ongoing delivery risk remains.
findings.figures: Multiple projects described as AMBER or experiencing delays throughout 2025/26
findings.quote: Chairs noted that the complexity of major projects, arising from factors such as funding and road management, can lead to delays. Chairs recommend that timescales are set more realistically from the outset.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Annual Wellbeing Report Appendix 3a Performance Panel Letter, Recommendations and Observations
findings.headline: EV charging infrastructure delivery slow and at risk of funding loss due to procurement contractual issues.
findings.detail: The council's electric vehicle charging infrastructure project is experiencing slow progress and faces risk of funding loss. Scrutiny expressed concern about the potential loss of funding, with delays attributed to contractual issues arising from the procurement process.
findings.matters: An infrastructure investment program is at risk of losing funding due to delivery delays and procurement problems; this signals both cash flow and project execution risk.
findings.figures: No specific delivery or funding figures provided
findings.quote: Chairs noted that progress has been slow in delivering additional charging points and were concerned about the potential loss of funding, they noted the response regarding contractual issues following the procurement process as causing delays.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Annual Wellbeing Report Appendix 3a Performance Panel Letter, Recommendations and Observations
findings.headline: Indoor Market restoration project delayed; council unable to align funding with essential upgrade costs.
findings.detail: The Indoor Market restoration project has not commenced, with the council unable to align available funding with the full cost of essential upgrade works. This has caused a consequential delay to the completion date, which was originally scheduled for September 2027.
findings.matters: A planned capital project cannot proceed due to funding/cost misalignment; this indicates capital planning issues and signals execution risk on other schemes.
findings.figures: Originally scheduled: September 2027 completion
findings.quote: Chairs note the delay in the commencement of the Indoor Market restoration project is due to issues aligning funding with the costs of essential upgrade work, meaning there will be a consequential delay in completion, which was originally scheduled for September 2027.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Annual Wellbeing Report Appendix 3a Performance Panel Letter, Recommendations and Observations
findings.headline: Into Work Services funding ends after 2026-27; clarity on successor funding not expected until December 2026.
findings.detail: The council's Into Work Services are currently funded through the Shared Prosperity Fund and Local Growth Funding, both ending after 2026-27. Scrutiny noted funding uncertainty and potential restructuring needs, with clarity on alternative funding expected by December 2026. The panel recommended the funding uncertainty be included in the Annual Well-being Report's risk section.
findings.matters: A well-performing service faces confirmed funding ending in 2026-27 with successor funding unconfirmed; delay in securing clarity by December carries service restructuring and continuity risk.
findings.figures: Clarity expected December 2026; current funding ends after 2026-27
findings.quote: Members queried whether this funding would continue and note that funding for Into Work services is under review, that the Council is hoping for greater clarity by December 2026, that alternative funding is being explored and that this is being kept under active watch.

findings.headline: Capital financing costs rising: PWLB borrowing rates remain in excess of 6% with significant future borrowing requirement.
findings.detail: The council's main borrowing source (PWLB) remains above 6% in the long term. With substantial future capital investment planned (including arena, housing programme) and Capital Financing Requirement growing, capital financing costs are forecast to increase significantly over the medium term. Even existing commitments carry interest rate risk if rates remain elevated.
findings.matters: Higher capital financing costs reduce headroom in revenue budget and increase long-term cost exposure. Council's ability to fund capital programme depends on sustained revenue budget pressure management and continued access to PWLB.
findings.figures: PWLB rates in excess of 6% for long-term borrowing
findings.quote: Whilst interest rates fluctuate with economic cycles, the rates at which the Council can borrow in the long term remain in excess of 6%.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account budget gap of £1.576m for 2027/28 will require drawdown of HRA reserves.
findings.detail: The HRA has an estimated budget gap of £1.576m for 2027/28 and £10.62m over the MTFP period, even after allowing for £4.16m targeted efficiency savings and service change. The gap will be funded from HRA earmarked reserves in the medium term. Council will need to develop detailed efficiencies plan to address this. Non-achievement of efficiency savings will further deplete reserves.
findings.matters: HRA reserve depletion is a sign of housing service financial stress. If reserves deplete, HRA may need to cut investment or raise rents further, both of which have policy/service implications.
findings.figures: £1.576 million HRA budget gap 2027/28; £10.62 million over MTFP; £4.16 million efficiency savings/service change assumed
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget and MTFP indicated a temporary budget gap for the HRA, estimated at £1.576 million for 2027/28 and £10.62 million over the MTFP period, after assuming targeted efficiency savings and service change estimated at £4.16 million.

findings.headline: Regional Integration Fund (£8m+ annually) confirmed only to end 2026/27; future funding uncertain.
findings.detail: Cardiff receives over £8m annually from Regional Integration Fund to support key social services areas. Funding is only confirmed to 31 March 2027. Future arrangements are not yet decided, creating medium-term funding uncertainty. Council notes that if large-scale grant reductions occur, it will not be possible to make them good and service levels will need to be reviewed.
findings.matters: A £8m+ funding cliff at end of 2026/27 could create major budget shortfall if not replaced. This is a specific, material grant risk that would affect 2028/29 budget and beyond. Lender needs clarity on council's contingency.
findings.figures: £8 million+ annual revenue from Regional Integration Fund
findings.quote: Particular areas to keep under close review for 2027/28 include future arrangements for Regional Integration Fund (RIF) which supports key areas of Social Services, but which is only confirmed in its current form until the end of 2026/27. Cardiff currently receives over £8 million of revenue funding annually from RIF.

findings.headline: Welsh Government 2027/28 settlement not yet confirmed; each 1% variance equates to £7.2m.
findings.detail: The council's 2027/28 MTFP assumes 2% AEF increase but no settlement has been issued. Provisional settlement expected November 2026, final February 2027. The 2026/27 settlement provided no indicatives beyond that year. A 1% shortfall from assumptions would cost £7.2m against a £4m Financial Resilience Mechanism buffer, leaving 0.5% protection. This is a material funding risk.
findings.matters: Lender exposure depends partly on whether funding shortfalls create additional borrowing need. If AEF is 1% below assumption, the council faces £7.2m unbudgeted shortfall with limited buffer.
findings.figures: £7.2 million per 1% AEF variance; £4 million Financial Resilience Mechanism; 0.5 percentage points coverage
findings.quote: In cash terms, each 1% difference in AEF equates to almost £7.2m. As such the absence of indicatives presents a key risk to planning assumptions both in terms of distribution and quantum, as a result of changes in indicators such as movements in population relative from one Council to another.

findings.headline: Care home recommissioning will cost up to £4m in 2027/28 and commit council in advance of budget approval.
findings.detail: New care home framework rates would cost £2.8m full year (£2.6m in 2027/28). Inflation adjustment adds further £1.4m (estimated). Commissioning timeline means providers will be notified of rates during 2026/27, effectively committing the council to these costs before the 2027/28 budget is formally approved. Paper includes recommendation for council to agree this expenditure in advance.
findings.matters: This represents both demand pressure (real cost increase) and governance risk (committing expenditure before budget approval). For a lender, it signals potential for further uncontrolled cost pressures in social care.
findings.figures: £2.8 million full-year impact; £2.6 million 2027/28; £1.4 million additional inflation adjustment; £4 million total recommended for approval
findings.quote: If the current proposed framework rates are implemented, the estimated cost impact would be £2.8 million in a full year, and based on a May 2027 launch date, £2.6 million of this would fall in 2027/28... at the point of disclosure to Providers, the intention is that these will be adjusted for estimated 2027/28 inflation; based on current RLW and CPI assumptions this is estimated to add a further £1.4 million to costs in 2027/28.

findings.headline: Savings achievement declining: 85% in 2025/26, down from 92% in 2022/23.
findings.detail: The council achieved only 85% of planned savings in 2025/26, down from 84% in 2023/24 and 92% in 2022/23. With savings requirements of £34.6m needed for 2027/28 alone and £118.9m over the MTFP, declining achievement rates raise risk of further shortfalls. Council states unachieved savings must be delivered in current financial year.
findings.matters: If a council cannot deliver 85% of modest savings, lender confidence in delivery of £119m savings over MTFP period should be low. This is a leading indicator of budget control and implementation capability.
findings.quote: The percentage of savings achieved was 85% for 2025/26 (this is slightly higher than 2024/25 which was 79%, but lower than earlier years – with 84% achievement in 2023/24 and 92% in 2022/23.)

findings.headline: Schools moving into cumulative deficit of £9.6m by March 2027; aggregate balance was £5.4m surplus at March 2026.
findings.detail: School governors' approved budgets for 2026/27 now project a £9.6m cumulative deficit by 31 March 2027. This represents a £15m swing from the £5.4m surplus position at end of March 2026. Schools pressures form a significant part of the £45m budget gap for 2027/28. Pressures are driven by ALN funding (50% of school pressures), pupil number growth in complex needs, and unfunded pay awards.
findings.matters: A swing from £5.4m reserves to £9.6m deficit in school finances signals deterioration in a major service area and raises questions about council's ability to manage education budget pressures. Lender needs confidence that this is manageable within overall financial strategy.
findings.figures: £9.6 million cumulative deficit projected 31 March 2027; £5.4 million aggregate balance 31 March 2026
findings.quote: Schools have finalised their Governor approved Budgets for 2026/27, and these reflect a projected cumulative deficit of £9.6 million by 31st March 2027.

findings.headline: Budget gap increased from £43.8m to £45.0m for 2027/28 and £163.7m over medium term.
findings.detail: The 2027/28 budget gap has worsened by £1.2m since March 2026 due to updated price inflation and demand projections. The four-year MTFP gap is £163.7m, comprising £60.4m in additional costs offset by £15.3m funding increases. This requires savings of £34.6m in 2027/28 (modelled gap excluding council tax increases of £10.4m).
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the scale of the budget challenge and trend (worsening, not improving). £163.7m over four years is substantial and shows the council faces sustained structural deficit.
findings.figures: £45.012 million 2027/28; £163.705 million 2027/28–2030/31; £43.810 million March 2026 forecast
findings.quote: Based on the considerations outlined above, the table below sets out the indicative budget gap for 2027/28, which is estimated at £45.012 million. This comprises additional costs of £60.352 million offset by net funding increases of £15.340 million. This is a £1.2 million increase compared with earlier forecasts.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Annual Wellbeing Report Appendix 5a Governance and Audit Committee Letter
findings.headline: Council faces a challenging financial environment with demand pressures and resource constraints, relying on transformational change programme.
findings.detail: The Committee acknowledges the Council operates within a challenging financial environment characterised by continuing demand pressures and resource constraints. The Council recognises that successful delivery of transformational change will be increasingly important to achieve objectives. Identified future challenges include the transition from Shared Prosperity Fund arrangements, maintaining the school estate, and delivering major digital and information technology programmes.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that a council can maintain service delivery and meet debt repayment obligations within resource constraints and rising demand. The council's identification of challenges and commitment to transformation is material to financial sustainability.
findings.quote: successful delivery of transformational change will become increasingly important in supporting the achievement of Council objectives within a challenging financial environment characterised by continuing demand pressures and resource constraints

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Annual Wellbeing Report Appendix 5a Governance and Audit Committee Letter
findings.headline: Governance and Audit Committee confirms governance arrangements are effective and corporate risks are being managed.
findings.detail: The Committee is satisfied with the Council's governance framework and self-assessment process. Governance arrangements are clear, consistently applied, and informed by data and evidence. Corporate risks outside target tolerance are appropriately reflected in the self-assessment, showing effective alignment between risk management and performance evaluation. The Panel Performance Assessment describes Cardiff as a well-run local authority.
findings.matters: Sound governance and risk management provide assurance that the council can identify and manage financial and operational challenges, which is essential for debt repayment capability.
findings.quote: We noted that the governance arrangements supporting corporate planning, performance monitoring and review are clearly defined, consistently applied and informed by a wide range of data sources, evidence and stakeholder perspectives.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Annual Wellbeing Report Appendix 3b - Cabinet Response to Performance Panel Recommendations
findings.headline: Seven schools requiring urgent and substantial repair works indicating capital spending pressure
findings.detail: At the end of quarter 3 2025/26, seven schools were categorised as requiring urgent and substantial repair works. This represents an identified capital maintenance obligation. The Cabinet clarified this is separate from one Category D 'end-of-life' school.
findings.matters: Significant school condition issues create future capital spending obligations that affect medium-term financial planning, reserves deployment, and may influence borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: 7 schools requiring urgent and substantial repair works at end of Q3 2025/26
findings.quote: Seven schools were categorised as requiring urgent and substantial repair works at the end of Quarter 3.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Annual Wellbeing Report Appendix 3b - Cabinet Response to Performance Panel Recommendations
findings.headline: Cycle Hangar scheme significantly exceeding cost assumptions and missing delivery targets
findings.detail: By end of quarter 4, only 17 cycle hangars had been installed against a target of 50. The Panel noted the scheme is 'one of the most expensive' in Cardiff. The council is actively reviewing costs with work ongoing to reduce both capital expenditure and annual operating fees, and will reimburse residents if fees are reduced. Remaining 10 hangars are planned for August/September installation with final 23 targeted for completion by November.
findings.matters: A capital project experiencing significant cost overruns and delivery delays indicates potential cost control issues, and the council's active need to reduce costs suggests the original spend assumption was substantially misjudged.
findings.figures: 17 installations versus 50 target; remaining 10 planned August/September; remaining 23 targeted November
findings.quote: Chairs note that the scheme in Cardiff is one of the most expensive and that this is being reviewed with the remaining hangars due to be delivered by the Autumn.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Annual Wellbeing Report Appendix 3b - Cabinet Response to Performance Panel Recommendations
findings.headline: Into Work Services identified as having funding uncertainty requiring potential restructure
findings.detail: The Panel noted funding uncertainties affecting Into Work Services and advised that a restructure may be needed. The Cabinet has amended the Annual Wellbeing Report to include this funding uncertainty in the Areas of Challenge and Risk section for Wellbeing Objective 3, and will involve the Economy & Culture Scrutiny Committee early in discussions shaping the service's way forward.
findings.matters: Funding discontinuity and service restructuring can affect both the council's cash requirements and its ability to deliver employment support programmes that may influence borrowing capacity and expenditure planning.
findings.figures: Into Work Services identified as having funding uncertainties
findings.quote: Chairs note the funding uncertainties for this area and that a restructure may be needed and welcome your support for the Economy & Culture Scrutiny Committee being involved early on in discussions shaping the way forward.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Annual Wellbeing Report Appendix 4a - Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee Letter
findings.headline: Indoor arena capital project remains on track to open in late 2028 with expected substantial economic benefits.
findings.detail: Committee noted the arena is considered a significant success story for Cardiff. It is expected to bring substantial economic benefits, support jobs in the hospitality sector, and contribute to regeneration of the surrounding area.
findings.matters: Successful major project delivery on schedule demonstrates capital management capability and expected future economic returns that should support council finances.

findings.headline: New borrowing at above 6% rates in medium and long term against £1.7 billion borrowing requirement.
findings.detail: Existing borrowing is fixed-rate and not immediately affected by rate changes, but all new borrowing will be at higher rates. The council states: 'Interest rates are expected to fall however inflation risks and concerns about increasing levels of national borrowing are resulting in medium and longer term rates being above 6%.' With £1.7bn projected borrowing need, the cost impact from elevated rates on new tranches is material.
findings.matters: New borrowing at 6%+ rates against a massive planned borrowing requirement creates foreseeable revenue pressure; even modest rate improvements would not likely return to historical lows.
findings.figures: rates forecast above 6% medium/long-term; applies to circa £1.7 billion projected borrowing need

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Appendix 1. Budget Strategy QA 27.28
findings.headline: Capital borrowing requirement forecast to reach circa £1.7 billion by 2029/30 with revenue financing cost implications.
findings.detail: The current capital strategy assumes the borrowing requirement will reach around £1.7bn by 2029/30 'assuming the investment plan is delivered'. The council has outlined the mechanics: 'each £1 million of capital expenditure places additional pressure of £100,000 on the revenue budget' (assuming 25-year asset life). At £1.7bn borrowing, this implies £170m+ in annual revenue pressure for capital financing costs. This cascades onto an already-pressured revenue budget.
findings.matters: A material projected increase in borrowing with direct and proportionate impact on revenue budget; at £1.7bn, the annual revenue cost alone could exceed the entire 2027/28 budget gap.
findings.figures: circa £1.7 billion borrowing by 2029/30; £1 million capital = £100,000 annual revenue cost (25-year assumption); implies £170+ million annual revenue pressure
findings.quote: The current capital strategy assumes that the requirement to borrow will increase to circa £1.7 billion by 2029/30, assuming the investment plan is delivered.

findings.headline: Pay award cost pressure of £17.4 million for 2027/28 based on estimates as pay awards remain unconfirmed.
findings.detail: Pay represents the second-largest cost driver after inflation. The council forecasts £17.4m from pay awards affecting teachers (teachers' pay award) and 'most other Council workers including social workers, refuse collectors, teaching assistants, midday supervisors, and office staff' under the NJC award. Critically, 'Pay awards are not yet agreed for 2027/28, so figures are based on estimates.' This creates upside risk to the deficit.
findings.matters: A major cost pressure (29% of the gap) based on estimates not yet agreed, creating material risk to budget assumptions.

findings.quote: £17.4 million for estimated pay awards. Workforce is a key driver of cost and so we need to consider the impact of pay awards. Most, although not all, Council staff are covered by two key awards – the teachers' pay award and the NJC award which covers most other Council workers including social workers, refuse collectors, teaching assistants, midday supervisors, and office staff. Pay awards are not yet agreed for 2027/28, so figures are based on estimates.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Appendix 1. Budget Strategy QA 27.28
findings.headline: Demand-driven cost growth of £11.3 million in adult and children's social care with rising complexity compounding unit cost increases.
findings.detail: Social care demand is growing in both numbers and complexity. The council forecasts £11.3m additional cost for 'increase in the number of people needing our support in Adult and Children's Social Care' plus education demand including pupil numbers, additional learning needs and transport. The paper explicitly notes: 'Demand for services is one of the most difficult areas to predict. As well as increasing numbers, complexity of demand is also having a significant cost impact.'
findings.matters: Demand-driven cost is structural and difficult to contain through efficiency alone; growing complexity signals rising per-unit costs, not just volume.

findings.quote: £11.3 million for anticipated demand increases. This reflects an increase in the number of people needing our support in Adult and Children's Social Care. It also includes education-related costs like changing pupil numbers, additional learning needs, and school transport pressures. Demand for services is one of the most difficult areas to predict.
