findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Appendix 1. Budget Strategy QA 27.28
findings.headline: Service delivery changes and reductions signalled as necessary, with efficiency savings alone unable to bridge the gap.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it cannot balance the budget through efficiency savings alone. The paper confirms: 'The scale of savings required is such that it will not be possible to balance the budget through efficiency savings alone and there will be a need for changes that impact on service delivery. These will be consulted on in coming months.' Of the £45.0m 2027/28 gap, only £34.6m is to come from savings, with the remainder (£10.4m) from a 4.95% council tax increase modelled.
findings.matters: Signals that the council is moving beyond cost-cutting to service restructuring and reduction, a material shift in delivery model.
findings.figures: £34.6 million savings required 2027/28; £10.4 million from 4.95% council tax increase (modelled); £118.9 million total savings over four years
findings.quote: The scale of savings required is such that it will not be possible to balance the budget through efficiency savings alone and there will be a need for changes that impact on service delivery. These will be consulted on in coming months.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Appendix 1. Budget Strategy QA 27.28
findings.headline: Medium-term budget deficit of £163.7 million over four years from £223.7 million cost pressures against £60.0 million funding.
findings.detail: The 2027/28 deficit is not isolated. The council's Medium Term Financial Plan shows a four-year structural gap of £163.7m: 2028/29 £35.4m, 2029/30 £37.6m, 2030/31 £45.7m. Cost pressures rise to £223.7m cumulatively while funding increases remain constrained at £60.0m across the period.
findings.matters: Demonstrates a sustained structural deficit, not a one-year anomaly. The scale and persistence of the gap signals continued service delivery pressure across the medium term.
findings.figures: £163.7 million total four-year gap; £223.7 million cost pressures; £60.0 million funding increases; year-by-year: 2027/28 £45.0m, 2028/29 £35.4m, 2029/30 £37.6m, 2030/31 £45.7m
findings.quote: Yes, the budget gap is estimated to be £163.7 million in total over the next four years. This is made up of estimated cost pressures totalling £223.7 million compared with estimated funding increases for £60.0 million.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Appendix 1. Budget Strategy QA 27.28
findings.headline: Revenue budget gap of £45.0 million for 2027/28 driven by £60.3 million cost pressures against uncertain funding.
findings.detail: The council faces a confirmed £45.0m gap for 2027/28 from cost increases of £60.3m against funding increases of only £15.3m. The £14.3m general grant increase in the funding assumption is based on an unconfirmed 2% rise; no indicative settlement has been received from Welsh Government yet. Each 1% variance in grant funding equals £7.2m impact. Welsh Government's draft budget expected 17 November; provisional settlement date not yet set.
findings.matters: A material unfunded deficit requiring immediate action, with funding assumptions remaining unconfirmed just months before the 11 March 2027 budget-setting deadline.
findings.figures: £45.0 million gap, £60.3 million costs, £15.3 million funding, £14.3 million assumed grant (assumes 2%), £7.2 million per 1% grant variance

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Annex 1 - Medium Term Financial Plan 2027.28 - 2030.31
findings.headline: Section 117 Aftercare Supreme Court ruling (August 2023) creates unfunded out-of-county placement risk for Cardiff due to concentration of specialist care providers in the city
findings.detail: The ruling changes responsibility for aftercare following compulsory mental health detention from the placing authority to the 'ordinarily resident' authority. Cardiff has a high number of specialist care providers; many out-of-county individuals placed in Cardiff will now become Cardiff's financial responsibility for ongoing aftercare. The council describes this as 'a financial risk for Cardiff.'
findings.matters: This is a new unfunded liability created by a Supreme Court ruling. The council has no funding allocation to cover it and cannot easily model the scale. It represents uncontrollable cost growth linked to the location of specialist provision.
findings.figures: No quantified impact provided
findings.quote: This represents a financial risk for Cardiff because there are a high number of specialist care providers in the city that accommodate those with significant and complex needs.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Annex 1 - Medium Term Financial Plan 2027.28 - 2030.31
findings.headline: Scenario modelling spans from £17m gap (optimistic: high growth, low inflation) to £290m gap (pessimistic: low growth, high inflation, high demand, cash-flat funding); base case £163m sits within a wide range of plausible outcomes
findings.detail: The council modelled 15 scenarios combining five economic scenarios with three demand scenarios. The optimistic outcome (high growth, low inflation, low demand) generates only £17m gap. The worst case (low growth, high inflation, high demand, cash-flat funding) generates £290m gap. The base case of £163m is acknowledged as sitting in the middle of a plausible range, not as a ceiling.
findings.matters: The width of the scenario range quantifies the council's financial uncertainty. The base case plan is contingent on a particular set of economic and demand outcomes. A lender needs to understand that the actual outcome could be substantially worse, requiring a materially different response.
findings.figures: Scenario range: £17m (optimistic) to £290m (pessimistic); base case £163m; average across all 15 scenarios: £154m
findings.quote: The £290 million and £17 million whilst extremes, are not implausible. The £290 million scenario reflects a combination of high inflation & low economic growth, coupled with higher demand and cash flat AEF.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Annex 1 - Medium Term Financial Plan 2027.28 - 2030.31
findings.headline: Council reserves at the lower end of adequacy for an authority of this size, with only £1m per annum budgeted from reserves and earmarked reserves already allocated
findings.detail: The council states: 'As a percentage of gross revenue expenditure, Cardiff has one of the lowest levels of reserves compared to other Welsh Authorities.' It is using £1m per annum of Strategic Budget Reserve as general funding and relying on earmarked reserves (many already committed to specific purposes) to manage volatility and to accommodate projected school deficits. This severely limits the council's ability to absorb economic shocks or funding surprises.
findings.matters: Reserve levels are a direct measure of financial resilience. Low reserves mean the council has limited shock absorption. Any adverse scenario (funding cut, demand spike, cost overrun) will require immediate service cuts rather than being managed across one or two years.
findings.figures: Annual general reserve use: £1m; total budgeted use of reserves across MTFP: £4m; school deficit accommodation requires temporary earmarked reserve use
findings.quote: The level of reserves held by Cardiff Council may be considered to be just at an adequate level for an Authority of this size. As a percentage of gross revenue expenditure, Cardiff has one of the lowest levels of reserves compared to other Welsh Authorities.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Annex 1 - Medium Term Financial Plan 2027.28 - 2030.31
findings.headline: Cardiff's population growing faster than other Welsh authorities; levy contributions will increase above average, particularly South Wales Fire & Rescue Service contribution of £25.5m
findings.detail: Cardiff's population has grown 7.9% since 2021 (28,000 people), compared to 4.2% growth across all Wales 2011–2021. Projected further growth of 6.9% to 414,900 by 2035. The South Wales Fire & Rescue Service levy is distributed on a population basis; as Cardiff's share of the regional population grows, its levy share grows above the average for constituent authorities.
findings.matters: This is a structural cost pressure the council cannot control. As the city grows, the cost base grows automatically. This compounds the gap problem: population growth drives demand (schools, social care) and external levy costs, but funding growth is not allocated on a population-proportionate basis.
findings.figures: Cardiff population 2021–2025: +28,000 (7.9%); Wales 2011–2021: +4.2%; projected Cardiff growth 2025–2035: +6.9% to 414,900; SWFRS current levy £25.5m
findings.quote: As Cardiff's population is anticipated to increase faster than that of other Local Authorities, it is likely that Cardiff's annual increases will be above the average.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Annex 1 - Medium Term Financial Plan 2027.28 - 2030.31
findings.headline: Additional Learning Needs demand at exceptional levels; out-of-county placement costs forecast to increase annually despite expansion of in-county specialist capacity
findings.detail: ALN contributes £44.2m of the total £224m demand pressure forecast over the MTFP. Special schools and specialist resource bases generate £18.9m pressure alone. Despite plans to increase specialist placements in council-maintained schools, the council is forecasting continued annual increases in out-of-county placements due to 'exceptional levels of demand and sustained referrals.' Complexity of cases is rising (more residential rather than foster placements), and the foster care market has contracted.
findings.matters: This is a demand pressure the council cannot control and cannot mitigate through its own capacity expansion. Costs will continue to rise. The council explicitly states it cannot assume any reduction in out-of-county demand despite adding specialist places, which signals that demand is outpacing its ability to accommodate in-county.
findings.figures: ALN demand pressure £44.2m total; special schools and SRBs £18.9m; mainstream pupil number savings offset by ALN growth; percentage of CLA in residential settings rising (from chart: 8–15% over recent years)
findings.quote: Currently however, due to exceptional levels of demand, and sustained referrals for specialist placements, no reduction in the annual level of demand for out of county placements has been assumed, with costs forecast to increase annually over the MTFP.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Annex 1 - Medium Term Financial Plan 2027.28 - 2030.31
findings.headline: Commissioned care costs rising faster than funding settlements, creating an unfunded structural pressure in a £200m+ budget
findings.detail: The council is planning Real Living Wage increases to commissioned care workers (5.5% in 2027/28, stepping down to 4.0% by 2030/31) to ensure care providers can pay the RLW. However, the MTFP states explicitly: 'The annual price increases factored into the MTFP for commissioned care are higher than anticipated AEF increases over the medium term and therefore represent an unfunded pressure.' This is a permanent structural mismatch in a budget spanning Adults and Children's Services.
findings.matters: This is an identified unfunded pressure with no mitigation strategy. The council is choosing to fund care worker pay rises but is not receiving corresponding funding increases. As the budget continues to consume more of total expenditure, this unfunded gap will compound.
findings.figures: Commissioned care budget >£200m across Adults and Children's Services; RLW assumptions 5.5%, 5.0%, 4.5%, 4.0% annually; projected RLW rate £14.19, £14.90, £15.57, £16.19
findings.quote: The annual price increases factored into the MTFP for commissioned care are higher than anticipated AEF increases over the medium term and therefore represent an unfunded pressure.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Annex 1 - Medium Term Financial Plan 2027.28 - 2030.31
findings.headline: Long-term Public Works Loan Board borrowing rates exceed 6%, up from historic lows, limiting capital investment affordability and creating long-term refinancing cost risk
findings.detail: PWLB rates have risen sharply from historic lows. The council is planning new capital borrowing at approximately 5%, but rates now exceed 6%. The council has significant future capital commitments and notes that interest rate changes will need close review. The plan assumes no new borrowing commitments funded by additional borrowing except where business cases show revenue income/savings will cover the cost.
findings.matters: The council's capital programme is funded partly by borrowing. If rates remain elevated or rise further, capital financing costs will exceed budget. This absorbs revenue resources that could otherwise go to services. The long maturity of capital debt means the impact extends 30+ years.
findings.figures: PWLB rates now exceed 6.0%; assumed rate for new borrowing ~5%; South Wales Fire & Rescue Service levy currently £25.5m
findings.quote: Whilst existing borrowing is at fixed rates, the significant future borrowing requirement linked to planned capital investment, means that there is a risk of increased costs well into the long term.

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Annex 1 - Medium Term Financial Plan 2027.28 - 2030.31
findings.headline: Schools projected to carry aggregate deficit of £9.6m by March 2027, with cumulative balance reduction of £27m since March 2022; council is using earmarked reserves to accommodate negative balances
findings.detail: Schools have burned through £27m of reserves in four years. The 2026/27 position is projected at a £9.6m aggregate deficit. The council is allowing negative school balances to persist by making temporary use of reserves that are already earmarked for other purposes. Individual schools are required to have approved recovery plans, but the trajectory is concerning.
findings.matters: School balance deficits indicate that delegated budgets are set at levels schools cannot sustain. Drawing on central reserves to cover this is a transfer of financial pressure from schools to the council. It limits financial flexibility and raises questions about the sustainability of the school funding strategy.
findings.figures: Cumulative reduction in school balances since 31 March 2022: £27m; projected aggregate deficit 31 March 2027: £9.6m
findings.quote: School Governor approved budgets set in May 2026, projected a cumulative deficit of £9.6million by 31 st March 2027

findings.paper_title: 2026-09-17 Budget Strat Annex 1 - Medium Term Financial Plan 2027.28 - 2030.31
findings.headline: Funding settlements are assumed at 2% per annum with no Welsh Government indicatives beyond 2026/27; a 1% variance equals £7.2m
findings.detail: The council is working from an assumption with no actual funding visibility. Each 1% shortfall in annual AEF represents £7.2m of additional savings needed. Scenario modelling shows that cash-flat funding (worst case) combined with high inflation and high demand would generate a £290m gap instead of the £163m base case.
findings.matters: A lender's confidence in the council's financial plan depends on knowing the scale of the assumption the plan rests on. With no firm settlement figures for four years and a sensitivity of £7.2m per percentage point, the council is publishing a plan with material hidden risk.
findings.figures: AEF assumption 2% p.a.; 1% variance = £7.2m; worst-case scenario (low growth, high inflation, cash-flat AEF) generates £290m gap vs. £163m base case

findings.headline: Adult Social Care budget grown 66% since 2020/21, now 20% of total council budget, with demographic pressures to 2035

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account faces £1.576m budget gap for 2027/28, requiring drawdown of HRA earmarked reserves

findings.matters: Reserve drawdown to cover recurring budget gaps is unsustainable; lenders monitor whether councils are using one-off reserves to plug structural deficits.
