findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Savings achievement rate declining while required savings growing to £119m over medium term
findings.detail: Savings achievement was 85% in 2025/26 (down from 92% in 2022/23, 84% in 2023/24). With the Council needing to find £119m in savings across the medium term (£34.6m in 2027/28 alone) to address the budget gap alongside modelled Council Tax increases, the declining achievement rate is a material concern. The council notes 'given the scale of savings requirements over the medium term, the importance of timely and robust savings planning cannot be underestimated.'
findings.matters: If savings delivery is declining, a council cannot be confident it will deliver the £119m needed, increasing the risk of in-year deficits.
findings.quote: The percentage of savings achieved was 85% for 2025/26 (this is slightly higher than 2024/25 which was 79%, but lower than earlier years – with 84% achievement in 2023/24 and 92% in 2022/23.)

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Local Growth Fund fell £3.3m year-on-year; revenue element down £6.9m requiring temporary funding plugs
findings.detail: In 2026/27, under LGF arrangements, Cardiff experienced a £3.312m reduction compared with 2025/26 SPF allocation. A recalibration towards capital meant this was heavily weighted to revenue with a £6.929m revenue reduction on 2025/26. The 2026/27 budget was balanced through a combination of base budget reallocation and temporary funding sources more than doubling available funding. Planning for 2027/28 will need to address 'ongoing arrangements for areas funded from temporary sources' and 'there may need for further reprioritisation of available funding, dependent on 2027/28 allocation.'
findings.matters: Grant funding volatility is forcing use of temporary funding to plug recurring revenue gaps.
findings.figures: 2026/27 reduction of £3.312m vs 2025/26, with £6.929m revenue reduction offset by temporary sources
findings.quote: In 2026/27, under LGF arrangements, Cardiff experienced a £3.312 million reduction in funding compared with its 2025/26 SPF allocation. A recalibration towards capital funding meant that this was heavily weighted to revenue with a £6.929 million reduction on 2025/26.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Regional Integration Fund (£8m+ annually) only confirmed to end of 2026/27; future arrangements unclear
findings.detail: The Council receives over £8 million of revenue funding annually from the Regional Integration Fund, which supports key areas of Social Services. This is identified as a 'key area' to keep under close review because it is only confirmed in its current form until the end of 2026/27. Given the council's dependency on specific grant funding and the risk of real-term reductions, this creates planning uncertainty.
findings.matters: Loss or reduction of £8m+ in social services funding would be material and could not simply be 'made good' from other sources.
findings.figures: Cardiff receives over £8 million of revenue funding annually from RIF
findings.quote: Another key area is Local Growth Fund which is set out in further detail in paragraphs 59-60. Particular areas to keep under close review for 2027/28 include future arrangements for Regional Integration Fund (RIF) which supports key areas of Social Services, but which is only confirmed in its current form until the end of 2026/27.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Teaching Assistant transition to Level 2 funding mechanism not confirmed; Welsh Government details still pending
findings.detail: Welsh Government has mandated that Level 1 Teaching Assistants transition to Level 2 from September 2026 to reflect changing responsibilities. Cardiff estimates limited cost for 2026/27 but costs will increase annually from April 2027 as staff increment through Grade 4. WG says it will provide funding but 'further detail of the formula and mechanism to be used to distribute this funding is not yet available.' The council notes 'the basis upon which the amounts will be distributed has not been confirmed, and therefore the financial implications of this to the Council will need to be kept under close scrutiny.'
findings.matters: A mandated cost increase with unconfirmed grant funding creates medium-term budget uncertainty.
findings.figures: All Teaching Assistants on Grade 3 moving to Grade 4; financial implications not fully quantified pending funding mechanism confirmation
findings.quote: Welsh Government have stated that funding will be provided to support this transition, though further detail of the formula and mechanism to be used to distribute this funding is not yet available. Whilst the current assumption is that specific grant would be provided in 2026/27 before transferring into the settlement in 2027/28, the basis upon which the amounts will be distributed has not been confirmed.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Capital programme restricted to essential legal/regulatory only; low receipts do not support affordability
findings.detail: The Council states that 'additional borrowing for new projects is deemed high risk' and that going forward, capital expenditure should be 'focussed on essential legal and regulatory requirements only.' The low level of capital receipts actually generated does not support affordability of the current programme. PWLB borrowing rates remain in excess of 6%, creating long-term revenue risk. The Council notes unrecovered expenditure on projects like the International Sports Village.
findings.matters: A sharp constraint on capital investment signals financial stress; lenders care about how councils are limiting future commitments.
findings.figures: PWLB rates in excess of 6%; General Fund capital receipts target: £2m per annum; ISV recovery costs still outstanding
findings.quote: additional borrowing for new projects is deemed high risk given external factors and therefore the approach to updating and formulating the investment programme in 2027/28 and over the medium term will be that any future capital expenditure would need to be focussed on essential legal and regulatory requirements only.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: School balances deteriorating; cumulative deficit projected to reach £9.6m by end of 2027
findings.detail: Aggregate school balances fell from £8.2m projected deficit (May 2025 forecast) to actual £5.4m positive by March 2026. However, for 2026/27, Governor-approved budgets now forecast a cumulative deficit of £9.6m by 31 March 2027. Both the number of schools in deficit and average deficit per school are rising. The council notes this 'will require a continued need for schools and Education to work closely together' to halt and reduce deficits 'over the next three years.'
findings.matters: School budget deficits constrain the authority's flexibility and signal persistent structural problems in education spending.
findings.figures: Aggregate balance March 2026: £5.4m; projected deficit 31 March 2027: £9.6m cumulative; number of schools in deficit and average deficit both projected to increase
findings.quote: Schools have finalised their Governor approved Budgets for 2026/27, and these reflect a projected cumulative deficit of £9.6 million by 31st March 2027... there are clear challenges in returning to a balanced position in the medium term.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Multiple specific grants at risk of reduction or discontinuation, including Regional Integration Fund confirmed only to March 2027
findings.detail: The paper identifies grant risks in: Universal Free School Meals (inflation coverage), Regional Integration Fund (confirmed only to March 2027), Sustainable Waste Management Grant (EPR risk), and Local Growth Fund (transitional year only). Historical pattern shows 'incidences where significant reductions in specific grants have occurred at short notice' where 'grants have been in place for a number of years'.
findings.matters: Loss of grant-funded services that have become 'core activity' could force emergency savings or budget rebalancing; multiple grants are at risk simultaneously.
findings.figures: No quantified figures disclosed; Regional Integration Fund confirmed only to March 2027
findings.quote: From a financial planning perspective, there is a risk that specific grants may reduce in cash or real terms or be discontinued altogether... Historically, there are incidences where significant reductions in specific grants have occurred at short notice.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Section 117 Supreme Court aftercare ruling creates new structural cost with no identified funding
findings.detail: The Council holds 'a high number of specialist care providers in the city that accommodate those with significant and complex needs'. A Supreme Court ruling means the Council where an individual is 'ordinarily resident' (prior to detention) now bears aftercare costs, not the placement authority. The ruling creates a new financial risk specific to Cardiff's position as a provider hub.
findings.matters: A single court ruling has shifted an undefined and potentially large cost stream to Cardiff due to its role as a specialist care provider centre, with no quantified impact or identified mitigation.
findings.figures: No quantified impact disclosed
findings.quote: This represents a financial risk for Cardiff because there are a high number of specialist care providers in the city that accommodate those with significant and complex needs.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Reserves described as 'just at an adequate level' and among lowest in Wales as percentage of spend
findings.detail: The Council holds one of the lowest reserve levels compared to peer Welsh authorities. The MTFP assumes £1.0m annual use of Strategic Budget Reserve for funding, and also plans temporary drawdown of earmarked reserves due to school deficits. A Financial Resilience Mechanism Budget of £4.5m is described as available to help manage funding settlement risk, but this is 'one-off' and could be reduced if required.
findings.matters: A council with tight reserves has limited buffer for unexpected cost or demand shocks, and limited financial flexibility to manage major changes in funding or cost assumptions.
findings.figures: £1.0m annual reserve use assumed; £4.5m Financial Resilience Mechanism Budget; Cardiff has one of lowest reserve levels in Wales
findings.quote: The level of reserves held by Cardiff Council may be considered to be just at an adequate level for an Authority of this size. As a percentage of gross revenue expenditure, Cardiff has one of the lowest levels of reserves compared to other Welsh Authorities.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: PWLB borrowing rates at 6%+ vs. MTFP assumption of ~5%, creating capital financing cost pressure
findings.detail: The paper notes 'PWLB rates now in excess of 6.0%' and 'there is a risk of increased costs well into the long term'. The MTFP assumes 'circa 5%' for new borrowing, an immediate 1%+ margin. Capital financing is growing as a budget component. The Council has also imposed a ceiling: 'No new commitments funded by additional borrowing in future years and a focus on securing external funding'.
findings.matters: Rising debt service costs directly reduce spending capacity and constrain capital programme affordability; the Council has already imposed a moratorium on new borrowing, signalling affordability concerns.
findings.figures: PWLB rates in excess of 6.0%; MTFP assumes circa 5%
findings.quote: Whilst interest rates fluctuate with economic cycles, there has been an increase from recent, historic lows, to long-term PWLB rates now in excess of 6.0%... Interest rate changes will need to be kept under close review, in terms of their impact on future capital financing budgets, and refinancing risk where borrowing is undertaken short-term.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Funding settlement assumption of 2% p.a. is major sensitivity; each 1% change equals £7.2m
findings.detail: The Council assumes 2% annual AEF increases through 2030/31 but notes 'there are currently no indicative funding figures for Welsh Local Government beyond 2026/27'. A 1% variance in AEF is worth £7.2m annually across the MTFP. Scenario analysis shows worst-case scenarios (low growth + high inflation + cash-flat AEF) create a £290m budget gap, nearly double the base case.
findings.matters: Funding assumptions carry material risk and one adverse settlement decision would require emergency savings equivalent to 1.5 years of planned reductions at current pace.
findings.figures: £7.2m sensitivity per 1% AEF; base case assumes 2% p.a.; worst-case scenario reaches £290m gap; current base £164m
findings.quote: There are currently no indicative funding figures for Welsh Local Government beyond 2026/27... The fact that funding figures are based, by necessity, on assumptions at this stage represents a material risk to the Council's financial resilience. This is because minor changes in AEF percentages have a significant impact in cash terms – with 1% of AEF equivalent to £7.2 million.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Commissioned care costs rising faster than funding, explicitly identified as unfunded pressure
findings.detail: The MTFP explicitly states 'The annual price increases factored into the MTFP for commissioned care are higher than anticipated AEF increases over the medium term and therefore represent an unfunded pressure.' Commissioned care budgets exceed £200m across adult and children's services. RLW assumptions are 5.5% in 2027/28 declining to 4.0% by 2030/31, well above CPI inflation assumptions of 1.9–2.0%.
findings.matters: An identified annual funding gap in services worth £200m+ signals structural budget stress that cannot be closed through one-off efficiency and represents a recurring annual pressure.
findings.figures: Commissioned care budget over £200m; RLW 5.5% 2027/28, CPI 1.9%
findings.quote: The annual price increases factored into the MTFP for commissioned care are higher than anticipated AEF increases over the medium term and therefore represent an unfunded pressure.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: School sector carrying aggregate deficit of £9.6m with recovery plan relying on 2028/29 improvement
findings.detail: Schools hold a projected cumulative deficit of £9.6m by March 2027. The Council plans to 'stop that deficit increasing further' and expects improvement in 2028/29, but the paper acknowledges 'there remains a need to consider the overall adequacy of reserves to accommodate this' and explicitly discusses 'carrying of negative school balances for the next two to three years'. Recovery timing and magnitude are uncertain.
findings.matters: School deficits consume council reserves that would otherwise be available for the general fund, reducing financial resilience and indicating structural budget stress in a sector representing 55% of spend.
findings.figures: £9.6m cumulative deficit by 31 March 2027; schools are 55% of council budget
findings.quote: School Governor approved budgets set in May 2026, projected a cumulative deficit of £9.6million by 31 st March 2027... the clear aim is to stop that deficit increasing further, plus an expectation that in 2028/29 aggregate school deficits will start to improve.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: £118.9m savings requirement with proposals not yet identified in detail
findings.detail: The Council must find £118.9m in savings over the MTFP period after assuming 4.95% annual council tax rises. The MTFP states that 'work on developing a fully defined set of proposals for the medium term, and in particular for 2027/28, has commenced', indicating proposals remain incomplete at budget planning time. This is a material delivery risk.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether identified pressures have credible, funded solutions or represent crystallising budget stress that may force unplanned borrowing or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £118.9m residual gap; £45.0m in 2027/28 alone
findings.quote: Work on developing a fully defined set of proposals for the medium term, and in particular for 2027/28, has commenced and will be supported by the service review and change programme in place to deliver savings and service improvement over the medium term.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Recommissioning of Adult Residential and Nursing Care flagged as significant budget risk requiring close review
findings.detail: The report identifies recommissioning work as "a significant risk area that will need to be kept under close review" and notes "the financial implications and timing of the Recommissioning of Adult Residential and Nursing Care" are material factors requiring a specific Council recommendation to progress "within the required timescales whilst adhering to budgetary framework."
findings.matters: Adult care commissioning is a major cost driver where timing and contract decisions can swing budgets significantly. Being flagged as a risk suggests material uncertainty.
findings.figures: none quantified in this document
findings.quote: Recommissioning Work - this is a significant risk area that will need to be kept under close review.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Arena commitment constrains capital borrowing; future capital spending restricted to essential legal and regulatory requirements only
findings.detail: The council prioritised the Arena as approved by Cabinet in November 2023, with costs recovered over 46 years from lease income. This "constrains future borrowing on other Major Projects in the medium term." The council's stated approach is to minimise new capital expenditure commitments and focus "on essential legal and regulatory requirements only," with major projects developer-funded.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand what capital exposure Cardiff is taking on and what growth investment capacity remains. The explicit constraint signals the council is managing debt risk tightly but limits regeneration.
findings.figures: Arena lease recovery period: 46 years
findings.quote: risk would be managed by prioritising investment and borrowing in the Arena. This constrains future borrowing on other Major Projects in the medium term and necessitates developer-led solutions.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Long-term borrowing rates exceed 6%, constraining capital affordability
findings.detail: The council's primary borrowing source is the Public Works Loan Board at fixed rates. The report states "the rates at which the Council can borrow in the long term are currently in excess of 6%" and notes that even without additional investment there are "risks linked to interest rates, capital receipts and inflationary pressure on existing schemes."
findings.matters: High PWLB rates directly reduce the affordability of capital investment and increase the burden on a revenue budget already facing a £45m gap.
findings.figures: rates "in excess of 6%"
findings.quote: the rates at which the Council can borrow in the long term are currently in excess of 6%

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Schools projected to run a cumulative deficit of £9.6 million by March 2027
findings.detail: Current modelling shows schools will be in deficit by £9.6m within six months. The council commits to work with Schools and Education to halt and then reduce both the size and number of schools in deficit over the next three years, but the deficit is a current reality.
findings.matters: School deficits signal a major budget area is not balanced and indicate resource transfer from elsewhere or future budget pressure.
findings.figures: £9.6 million cumulative deficit by 31st March 2027
findings.quote: current modelling projects a cumulative deficit of £9.6 million by 31st March 2027

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Budget gap of £45.012 million for 2027/28 requires £118.925 million in savings over four years, with service change likely needed
findings.detail: The council has identified a budget gap requiring almost £119m in directorate savings across the medium term, with over £34m needed for 2027/28 alone. The report explicitly states the council must "go beyond the traditional approach to identifying operational efficiencies" and service change proposals are "still likely to be required." Notably, the council achieved only 85% of its savings target in 2025/26.
findings.matters: A lender assessing Cardiff needs to understand whether this scale of savings is deliverable, especially given the prior year undershoot of 15%.
findings.figures: £45.012 million budget gap; £118.925m directorate savings required over MTFP; £34 million for 2027/28; 85% achievement rate in 2025/26
findings.quote: given that the level of savings required is almost £119 million across the medium term, and over £34 million for 2027/28 alone, it will be necessary go beyond the traditional approach to identifying operational efficiencies. the quantum of savings is such that options which impact on services (service change proposals) are still likely to be required.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Capital receipts from asset sales carry timing risk for large development projects
findings.detail: The council notes that capital investment plans include several major development projects dependent on capital receipts, but there is a risk where spending begins before receipts have been realised. This will need regular review as part of the annual property plan.
findings.matters: Timing mismatches between project spend and asset disposals can force unplanned borrowing or cash flow pressure.
findings.figures: Multiple major development projects dependent on capital receipts; risk of spending before receipts realised
findings.quote: There is a risk where spending begins before receipts have been realised, and this will need regular review as part of the annual property plan.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Future borrowing at risk from elevated interest rates; medium to long-term rates above 6%
findings.detail: Existing borrowing is at fixed rates and not immediately affected. However, future borrowing commitments mean new borrowing will be at higher rates. Medium and long-term rates are currently above 6%, and while rates are expected to fall, inflation risks and national borrowing levels pose downside risk.
findings.matters: Higher refinancing costs reduce the affordability of capital investment and add pressure to an already constrained revenue budget.
findings.figures: Medium and longer-term borrowing rates currently above 6%; new borrowing at higher rates than existing fixed-rate debt
findings.quote: Interest rates are expected to fall however inflation risks and concerns about increasing levels of national borrowing are resulting in medium and longer term rates being above 6%.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Capital borrowing requirement expected to reach £1.7 billion by 2029/30, placing sustained revenue pressure
findings.detail: The council expects borrowing to increase to circa £1.7bn by 2029/30. Each £1m of capital expenditure places approximately £100k of additional revenue pressure. Capital financing already accounts for a significant proportion of the revenue budget, and future borrowing at higher rates will increase that burden.
findings.matters: Large capital financing commitments compound revenue budget pressure and limit financial flexibility for a council already facing a structural deficit.
findings.figures: £1.7 billion borrowing requirement by 2029/30; £100,000 revenue impact per £1 million capital expenditure; rates expected above 6% medium to long term
findings.quote: The current capital strategy assumes that the requirement to borrow will increase to circa £1.7 billion by 2029/30, assuming the investment plan is delivered.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Social care demand is rising and becoming more complex, creating unpredictable cost pressure
findings.detail: The council anticipates demand increases of £11.3m for Adult and Children's Social Care, driven by both rising numbers and increasing complexity. The council notes that demand is one of the hardest areas to predict and that current-year performance directly affects the following year's forecast.
findings.matters: Demand-driven cost pressures in social care are difficult for councils to control and often exceed forecasts, creating ongoing revenue risk.
findings.figures: £11.3 million for anticipated demand increases in 2027/28; includes care for vulnerable children and adults
findings.quote: Demand for services is one of the most difficult areas to predict. As well as increasing numbers, complexity of demand is also having a significant cost impact.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Service delivery changes will be required; efficiency savings alone cannot close the gap
findings.detail: The council plans to save £34.6m in 2027/28 (£118.4m over four years) and assumes a 4.95% council tax increase (£10.4m). It explicitly states that efficiency savings and council tax alone are insufficient to balance the budget, and consultation on service delivery changes is coming.
findings.matters: Indicating that service reductions—which carry implementation risk, political risk, and may take time to realise—will be necessary alongside council tax rises.
findings.figures: £34.6 million savings required 2027/28; £118.4 million over 4 years; 4.95% council tax increase assumed (£10.4m)
findings.quote: The scale of savings required is such that it will not be possible to balance the budget through efficiency savings alone and there will be a need for changes that impact on service delivery.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Welsh Government funding for 2027/28 is not yet known, and small changes have large impact
findings.detail: The council assumes 2% increase in general grant but has no indicative allocation from Welsh Government. The Provisional Settlement will not be published until after the Welsh draft budget on 17 November, but the council must set a balanced budget by 11 March. Each 1% of general grant funding represents £7.2m.
findings.matters: Funding uncertainty of this scale, close to the budget-setting deadline, increases the risk of late-year reforecasting and makes medium-term planning difficult.
findings.figures: £7.2 million per 1% of general grant; £14.3 million assumed additional general grant (2% increase); Provisional Settlement timing uncertain
findings.quote: In short, we don't know. We don't have an indicative funding allocation for 2027/28 from Welsh Government yet.

findings.committee: Policy Review and Performance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Budget gap of £45.0 million for 2027/28, part of a £163.7 million gap over four years
findings.detail: The council faces estimated additional costs of £60.3m against funding increases of only £15.3m. This gap is driven by inflation pressures (£22.4m), demand increases in social care (£11.3m), and pay awards (£17.4m). Over the medium term, gross pressures total £223.7m against funding increases of £60.0m.
findings.matters: A structural budget gap of this scale requires significant service reductions and carries execution risk for a council already under revenue pressure.
findings.figures: £45.0 million gap 2027/28; £163.7 million over 4 years; £60.3 million cost pressures; £15.3 million funding increases
findings.quote: Yes, there is an estimated budget gap of £45.0 million for 2027/28. It reflects: Estimated additional costs of £60.3 million. Less, estimated funding increases of £15.3 million.

findings.headline: £267k management savings proposal remains unallocated and undelivered
findings.detail: The council budgeted £800k of management savings at the start of the year, with £633k held in Corporate Management pending finalisation of proposals. At outturn, £267k remains unallocated and undelivered. The council has stated it anticipates these will be achieved in 2026/27, but one year in they are still unallocated.
findings.matters: Unallocated savings that were planned but not specified suggest the council had no concrete plan to deliver them, and they now roll forward as a contingent saving.
findings.figures: £267,000 unallocated; £800,000 original proposal; £633,000 held pending finalisation
findings.quote: As reported in the 2025/26 Budget Report, there was a management savings proposal of £800,000, with the majority of this sum (£633,000) being held in Corporate Management, pending finalisation of proposals. At outturn, the unallocated management savings remained at £267,000, reflecting savings yet to be delivered but which are anticipated to be achieved in full next financial year.

findings.headline: Adult Services commissioned care overspend of £2.507m driven by demand for residential and respite placements
findings.detail: The council overspent on commissioned adult social care by £2.507m, with residential/nursing care up £926k and respite care up £649k. This is a demand-driven overspend that internal service underspends elsewhere in Adult Services (£3.541m) could only partially offset, leaving the directorate with a net underspend of £1.036m that masks an underlying structural issue.
findings.matters: Adult social care demand (particularly residential and respite) is rising faster than the council's budget and shows no sign of moderating. This is a structural pressure on the council's balance sheet.
findings.figures: £2.507 million overspend on commissioned care; Residential/Nursing £926,000 overspend; Respite Care £649,000 overspend
findings.quote: The £2.507 million overspend on Commissioned care includes overspends in Older People (£2.658m) and Substance Misuse (£267,000). In terms of types of care, the main areas of overspend were Residential / Nursing (£926,000) and Respite Care (£649,000).

findings.headline: £1.088m of planned savings went undelivered across three major directorates
findings.detail: Children's Services had £459k of unachieved savings; Adult Services £679k unachieved (though £453k expected in 2026/27); Planning, Transport & Environment £550k unachieved. These are not one-off slippages but indicate the council is struggling to deliver efficiency savings it has committed to, requiring offsetting elsewhere.
findings.matters: Repeated unachieved savings targets suggest either the savings plans are unrealistic or the council lacks delivery capacity, both of which affect financial forecasting reliability.
findings.figures: Children's Services: £2.567m target, £2.108m delivered (£459k shortfall); Adult Services: £4.273m target, £3.594m delivered (£679k shortfall); Planning Transport Environment: £2.463m target, £1.913m delivered (£550k shortfall)
findings.quote: Budgeted savings in Children's Services for 2025/26 totalled £2.567 million with £2.108 million achieved in the financial year. Shortfalls amounting to £459,000 primarily related to delays in further implementation of shifting the balance of care

findings.headline: City Hall closure delivered a £1.226m annual deficit in venue hire and catering
findings.detail: City Hall remained closed throughout 2025/26, making budgeted income targets unachievable. Functions Hire and Catering reported a £1.226m loss for the year. The service is now undergoing restructure to try to mitigate future shortfalls, but the income loss is structural while the building remains unavailable.
findings.matters: A major civic venue being offline for a full financial year creates a structural revenue hole and signals potential capital or operational issues with the building.
findings.figures: £1.226 million deficit; 100% of budgeted income not realised
findings.quote: Functions Hire and Catering reported a £1.226 million deficit as City Hall remained closed throughout the financial year rendering budgeted income targets unachievable. The service is undergoing a restructure to help mitigate future financial shortfalls arising from the continued closure.

findings.headline: Major Projects carries £173k of unfunded International Sports Village and Atlantic Wharf costs
findings.detail: A capital project initiative has accumulated costs with no identified funding source. The outturn shows £173k of International Sports Village and Atlantic Wharf related costs sitting in the revenue account against the Major Projects directorate, with no mechanism to fund them.
findings.matters: Unfunded capital-related costs in the revenue budget point to slippage in capital project delivery or cost overruns that were not planned for.
findings.quote: This included £173,000 of International Sports Village and Atlantic Wharf related costs with no other identified funding sources.

findings.headline: Children's residential care placements are 32% more expensive than those being replaced
findings.detail: The council faces structural cost escalation in residential care: new placements cost 32% more than the ones they replace. As of 31 March 2026, there are 114 ongoing places (up 6 from prior year). Four placements alone cost £16,500 per week. This created a £3.648m overspend in residential care. The model of care work mitigated some growth but the base cost is locked in higher.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether this council can control its largest social care cost. A 32% price inflation per replacement placement is a structural problem, not a temporary spike.
findings.figures: £3.648 million overspend; 32% cost differential; four placements at £16,500 per week; 114 ongoing places (up 6 year-on-year)
findings.quote: Within Children's Residential Care, the current cost position continues to reflect an increasing trend of elapsed placements being replaced by significantly more expensive new placements, with a cost differential of 32%. Since month 6, an increasing amount of care packages in excess of £10,000 a week has been experienced, with four high cost placements averaging £16,500 per week

findings.headline: Red Dragon Centre reserve now fully depleted after £1.5m deficit
findings.detail: The commercial property development reported a £1.5m loss driven by reduced rental income following expired leases where replacement tenants could not be secured. The council also granted Hollywood Bowl a six-month rent-free period. The reserve that has been absorbing these losses is now exhausted — £800k was drawn in-year with a £700k shortfall met from the directorate budget.
findings.matters: A reserve depletion signals the council can no longer absorb shocks to a major commercial income stream and has lost a buffer.
findings.figures: £1.500 million deficit; £800,000 drawn from reserve (now fully depleted); £700,000 shortfall met from directorate
findings.quote: Of this total, £800,000 was funded from the Red Dragon Centre Reserve, which has now been fully depleted, with the remaining £700,000 shortfall met within the directorate position.

findings.headline: Overall capital programme is 23% underspent, with £98m of general fund capital not deployed
findings.detail: The total General Fund capital programme was £422.5m but delivered only £324.2m, an underspend of £98m. This is not a single project failure but a systemic shortfall in capital delivery across the entire estate.
findings.matters: Large systematic underspend suggests the council either overcommits its capital programme, faces wider delivery bottlenecks (procurement, land, planning, financing), or has cash flow constraints that prevent deployment. Any of these signals governance or capacity issues to a lender.
findings.figures: TOTAL GENERAL FUND: £422,526k programmed, £324,231k outturn, (£98,057k underspend). Public Housing: £189,390k programmed, £149,855k outturn, (£39,535k underspend).
findings.quote: TOTAL GENERAL FUND

findings.headline: Housing capital programme is 21% underspent, with £39.5m not delivered across HRA schemes
findings.detail: Public Housing capital delivery fell £39.5m short of the £189.4m programme. New Builds and Acquisitions were £23.6m underspent (16%), and External and Internal Building Improvements underspent by £13.5m (39%). This affects both council housebuilding targets and stock maintenance.
findings.matters: Housing delivery is a statutory priority and affects the council's homelessness and housing strategy; large underspends suggest delays in acquisition, construction, or maintenance that may create social pressure and backlog.
findings.figures: PUBLIC HOUSING total programme £189,390k, outturn £149,855k, (£39,535k underspend). Housing - New Builds & Acquisitions: £148,090k programmed, £124,459k outturn, (£23,631k underspend).
findings.quote: Housing - New Builds & Acquisitions

findings.headline: School modernisation programme is half-delivered, with £58.6m underspent across two major schemes
findings.detail: Asset Renewal Suitability and Sufficiency schools programme: £50.1m budgeted, £24.8m delivered (50% underspend). 21st Century Schools Band B: £141.8m budgeted, £108.5m delivered (33% underspend). Together these add £33.3m of education capital slippage.
findings.matters: School modernisation is essential for council performance and statutory duty; large underspends suggest construction delays, planning issues, or phasing problems that may affect educational outcomes.
findings.figures: Asset Renewal, Suitability and Sufficiency: £50,095k programmed, £24,829k outturn, (£25,266k underspend). 21st Century Schools - Band B: £141,798k programmed, £108,477k outturn, (£33,321k underspend).
findings.quote: Asset Renewal, Suitability and Sufficiency

findings.headline: Energy retrofit programme has effectively stalled, delivering 0.4% of budget
findings.detail: The Energy REFIT Phase 4 - Tranche 1 project budgeted £1.985m but spent only £7k, an underspend of £1.978m. This is a climate/sustainability investment that has not progressed.
findings.matters: Stalled energy efficiency spending means future operating cost savings are not being realised; it also suggests either project cancellation, delay, or procurement failure in an area the council has committed to.
findings.figures: Energy REFIT Phase 4 - Tranche 1: £1,985k programmed, £7k outturn, (£1,978k underspend).
findings.quote: Energy REFIT Phase 4 - Tranche 1

findings.headline: New County Hall at Atlantic Wharf is 86% underspent, with only £809k delivered against a £5.8m budget
findings.detail: A major civic building project shows severe slippage: £5.8m was budgeted but only £809k was spent, leaving £5m undelivered. This appears to be a multi-year project carrying forward, but the scale of underspend suggests significant delays.
findings.matters: Major civic infrastructure delays can signal procurement, planning, or governance problems; the scale of underspend (86%) on a single project suggests it is substantially blocked or not yet mobilised.
findings.figures: New County Hall, Atlantic Wharf: £5,819k programmed, £809k outturn, (£5,010k underspend).
findings.quote: New County Hall, Atlantic Wharf

findings.headline: Indoor Arena has delivered only 45% of budgeted capital expenditure, with £27m of slippage across two schemes
findings.detail: The Land Assembly and Multi-Storey Car Park element delivered £9.9m of a £22m budget (55% underspend). The Direct Funding for Income Strip delivered £65.3m of an £80m budget (18% underspend). The Indoor Arena is Cardiff's flagship capital project; slippage at this scale on a scheme this large suggests either delivery difficulties or funding constraints.
findings.matters: A lender assesses council management capability through capital delivery; slippage this large on the council's marquee regeneration scheme signals delivery risk, and for a scheme relying on income generation, delays may defer revenue assumptions.
findings.figures: Indoor Arena - Land Assembly and Multi-Storey Car Park: £22,000k programmed, £9,880k outturn, (£12,120k underspend). Indoor Arena - Direct Funding for Income Strip: £80,000k programmed, £65,256k outturn, (£14,744k underspend).
findings.quote: Indoor Arena - Land Assembly and Multi-Storey Car Park

findings.headline: Capital programme experienced significant slippage of £137.826m (General Fund £98.291m + HRA £39.535m)
findings.detail: General Fund capital planned expenditure slipped by £98.291m and HRA by £39.535m. While the document attributes this to timing of projects and grants received late in the year, it indicates forecasting and delivery challenges on major schemes.
findings.matters: Large year-on-year slippage in capital delivery creates uncertainty about when major schemes will complete, impacts revenue budgets (through extended capital financing needs), and may indicate project management or funding coordination issues.
findings.figures: General Fund variance: £98.291m slippage. HRA variance: £39.535m slippage. Total combined slippage: £137.826m.
findings.quote: The Council continues to deliver a large and complex capital programme, influenced by many external and internal factors. Some slippage is unavoidable because of delays in projects due to planning and regulatory requirements, construction pressures etc

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement of £1.239 billion now exceeds external borrowing by £91m, requiring reliance on internal cash balances
findings.detail: The council is internally borrowed to the extent of £91 million, using internal cash balances rather than external borrowing to manage short-term costs. This approach is described as helping 'reduce costs in the short term' but indicates limited headroom between borrowing need and available funds.
findings.matters: Internal borrowing reduces available cash headroom and flexibility for managing unexpected financial shocks or acceleration of capital spending.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement: £1.239 billion. External borrowing: £1.148 billion. Internal borrowing: £91 million.
findings.quote: Whilst borrowing rates remained elevated in 2025/26, the Council was internally borrowed which means it was using internal cash balances in the short term rather than borrowing externally. This helped reduce costs in the short term.

findings.headline: External borrowing increased by £168m to £1.148 billion in a single year, with borrowing rates rising and described as 'elevated'
findings.detail: Total external debt at 31 March 2026 was £1.148 billion, up from £980 million at 31 March 2025. Unsupported borrowing of £157.073m was undertaken in 2025/26 alone, split between £28.884m to balance capital programme commitments and £128.189m for invest-to-save schemes. Average borrowing rate increased from 4.04% to 4.15% and document notes rates remain elevated.
findings.matters: A 17% increase in external debt in one year, primarily unsupported borrowing that must be repaid from future revenue, is a significant increase in financial risk, particularly as interest rates have been rising and are still described as elevated.
findings.figures: External borrowing 31 Mar 2026: £1,148m (vs £980m in 2025). Unsupported borrowing in 2025/26: £157.073m. Average borrowing rate increased from 4.04% to 4.15%. Interest payable: £43.8m.
findings.quote: In 2025/26, the Council used unsupported borrowing of £157.073 million to support General Fund expenditure. Of this, £28.884 million of borrowing was required to balance the Capital Programme commitments and £128.189 million was for investment assumed to be repayable from future Directorate revenue budgets.

findings.headline: Economic Development overspend of £1.482m reflecting income shortfalls and impact of office building closures
findings.detail: Income shortfalls in Functions and Catering services were 'still impacted by the closure of the core office buildings', plus unbudgeted premises holding costs at St David's Hall. This indicates ongoing structural cost issues from asset decisions rather than temporary operating problems.
findings.matters: Income-generating services facing structural demand loss due to property strategy decisions suggests a long-term pressure that cannot be quickly reversed.
findings.figures: Economic Development overspend: £1.482m. Income shortfalls in Functions and Catering impacted by office building closure. Unbudgeted premises holding costs at St David's Hall.
findings.quote: Income shortfalls primarily for Functions and Catering with the latter services still impacted by the closure of the core office buildings. There were also unbudgeted premises holding costs at St David's Hall

findings.headline: Children's Services overspend of £1.052m driven by external placement market volatility and agency staffing costs
findings.detail: Despite additional grant funding offsetting some pressures, the service reported an overspend largely due to external placement costs and agency staff levels required to meet operational needs. The document notes ongoing volatility in the market for external placements, indicating this is not a one-off issue.
findings.matters: Volatile market costs in children's placements are difficult to forecast and control. If growth in demand for external placements continues, this becomes a structural budget issue with limited council control.
findings.figures: Children's Services overspend: £1.052m. Overspends for external placements noted throughout year with ongoing volatility. Agency staff costs above budget within internally run Children's Residential Homes.
findings.quote: The position continued to reflect overspends for external placements, with ongoing volatility in the market. Further overspends included agency staff costs above budget within internally run Children's Residential Homes to meet required operational levels.

findings.headline: Savings targets missed by £2.262m (13.9% shortfall), with worsening performance in Service Change proposals
findings.detail: Against a total savings target of £16.261m, the council delivered £13.999m. Efficiency savings underperformed by 12% (£1.540m shortfall) but the more concerning figure is Service Change proposals at 24% shortfall (£0.722m). This suggests structural budget pressures are not being fully addressed through planned service changes.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether underfunding is being managed through identified, delivered savings or whether targets are wishful planning. A 24% miss on Service Change proposals indicates those changes are not being implemented as planned.
findings.figures: Total shortfall £2.262m against £16.261m target. Service Change proposals: £722k shortfall on £2.998m target (24% miss). Efficiency savings: £1.540m shortfall on £12.463m target (12% miss).
findings.quote: The performance against Efficiency savings proposals is a shortfall of £1.540 million and a further shortfall of £0.722 million for the Service Change proposals

findings.headline: Reserves are weak relative to council size; Cardiff has one of the lowest levels compared to other Welsh authorities
findings.detail: The MTFP notes explicitly that 'The level of reserves held by Cardiff Council may be considered to be just at an adequate level for an Authority of this size. As a percentage of gross revenue expenditure, Cardiff has one of the lowest levels of reserves compared to other Welsh Authorities.' The council uses £1m of reserves per year as general budget funding and plans temporary use of earmarked reserves (not needed until 2029/30) to cover school deficits.
findings.matters: Low reserves relative to budget size means less buffer against external shocks or delivery slippage. Limited room to absorb a funding settlement worse than assumed or a demand surge.
findings.figures: £1m annual use of reserves for general budget funding; temporary use of earmarked reserves planned for school deficit coverage
findings.quote: The level of reserves held by Cardiff Council may be considered to be just at an adequate level for an Authority of this size. As a percentage of gross revenue expenditure, Cardiff has one of the lowest levels of reserves compared to other Welsh Authorities.

findings.headline: Homelessness demand pressures to intensify; earmarked reserve funding is finite and WG legislative reform could increase costs materially
findings.detail: The MTFP notes 'significant pressures in homelessness' and uses earmarked reserve funding to supplement base budget, but warns 'longevity of this will be kept under close review.' The forthcoming Homelessness and Social Allocation (Wales) Bill is expected to require material capital and revenue implications, which are not currently reflected in the MTFP, with the expectation that WG will provide funding. A new grant stream for pre-implementation activity was introduced in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Homelessness demand is volatile and could spike if economic conditions worsen. Reliance on one-off reserves to manage it is unsustainable. Major legislation expected but funding and impact unquantified.
findings.figures: Homelessness budget: not separately quantified; current reserve support used; new WG grant stream introduced 2026/27 for pre-implementation activity
findings.quote: The MTFP also notes significant pressures in homelessness. Earmarked reserve funding is available to supplement base budget allocations to help manage demand. The longevity of this will be kept under close review, particularly in light of WG's Homelessness and Social Allocation (Wales) Bill.

findings.headline: Cardiff's population growth (6.9% to 2035) outpaces Wales average (4.2%), driving disproportionate levy cost increases
findings.detail: Cardiff's population is projected to grow 6.9% between 2025 and 2035, compared to 4.2% across all Welsh local authorities. Levies (particularly the South Wales Fire & Rescue Service at £25.5m current contribution) are distributed on a population basis. As Cardiff's population share increases, its levy contributions will grow faster than the average.
findings.matters: Faster population growth automatically increases a fixed-cost levy burden, reducing financial flexibility. This is a demographic headwind without offsetting service efficiency gains.
findings.figures: Cardiff population projection 2025–2035: +6.9% to 414,900; Wales average projection: +4.2%; SWFRS current council contribution: £25.5m
findings.quote: Between 2025 and 2035, Cardiff's population is projected to grow by a further 6.9% to 414,900 (compared to a projected increase of 4.2% across all local authorities in Wales). As Cardiff's population is anticipated to increase faster than that of other Local Authorities, it is likely that Cardiff's annual increases will be above the average.

findings.headline: Teachers' Pension Scheme (TPS) valuation due 2027 with uncertain implementation and funding assumptions unconfirmed
findings.detail: The Teachers' Pension Scheme valuation is expected in 2027 based on membership data as at 31 March 2024, but implementation date is uncertain given delays in the last two valuations. The MTFP assumes 'net nil impact' — that any increase would be matched by Welsh Government funding — consistent with the last two reviews. However, the council notes 'the position will need to be kept under close review.'
findings.matters: Teachers' pensions are already material post-2024 actuarial review. An unconfirmed valuation with implementation uncertainty and an assumption about WG funding that may not hold creates downside budget risk.
findings.figures: TPS contributions increased materially in September 2019 and again April 2024; next valuation expected 2027
findings.quote: At this stage, the MTFP is predicated upon the assumption that any change in Employer's contribution rate to the TPS linked to the 2024 actuarial review would be net nil in impact. In other words that any future increases would be matched via a funding allocation from Welsh Government, over and above core AEF assumptions outlined later in this document. This is consistent with what has happened at both of the last actuarial reviews, but the position will need to be kept under close review.

findings.headline: Section 117 Supreme Court aftercare ruling creates unquantified liability as Cardiff hosts high concentration of specialist care providers
findings.detail: A 2023 Supreme Court ruling on Section 117 Aftercare means Cardiff Council (where individuals were 'ordinarily resident' before detention) is responsible for aftercare provision for those placed out-of-county in specialist settings. Cardiff hosts a high number of specialist care providers, concentrating this liability. The financial impact is noted as unquantified but represents a material risk.
findings.matters: An unfunded liability with uncertain magnitude, concentrated in one council due to its geography. This is a contingent obligation that could crystallise with little warning.
findings.figures: No quantification provided; noted as 'a high number of specialist care providers in the city'
findings.quote: This represents a financial risk for Cardiff because there are a high number of specialist care providers in the city that accommodate those with significant and complex needs.

findings.headline: Additional Learning Needs (ALN) is now equivalent to or greater than social care as a cost pressure
findings.detail: The MTFP identifies a subtle shift in pressures whereby ALN has become an equivalent, if not greater pressure than social care. Demand for specialist placements is 'exceptional' with placements increasing within LA-maintained schools and out-of-county placements forecast to increase annually. Demand complexity continues to rise, and no reduction in out-of-county placement demand has been assumed.
findings.matters: A shifting high-cost demand driver that the council says is difficult to model and where it explicitly assumes no cost relief even as it builds internal capacity. This signals sustained cost growth in a less controllable area.
findings.figures: Demand pressure from ALN/special needs: £26.1m reduction from mainstream pupil numbers partially offset; actual net impact spread across retained education and delegated schools budgets
findings.quote: A similar graph over a longer period (10 years) would show Children's Services as the highest line. This is indicative of a subtle shift in recent years to a situation where Additional Learning Needs is becoming an equivalent, if not greater pressure than social care, although the latter remains material too.

findings.headline: Commissioned care costs (£200m+) facing unfunded pressure from Real Living Wage increases higher than anticipated AEF growth
findings.detail: The council's commissioned care budget across Adults and Children's Services exceeds £200m. Welsh Government committed that registered carers receive Real Living Wage, which the MTFP assumes will rise 5.5% in 2027/28, stepping to 4.0% by 2030/31. These increases outpace the assumed 2% AEF growth, creating an unfunded pressure. Material recommissioning risk exists (adult domiciliary and residential care due 2027/28) and price churn effects.
findings.matters: A £200m+ budget with annual cost pressures that exceed grant income growth is a core structural vulnerability. Recommissioning risk and price volatility compound the issue.
findings.figures: Commissioned care budget: >£200m across Adults and Children's Services; RLW 5.5% (2027/28), 5.0% (2028/29), 4.5% (2029/30), 4.0% (2030/31); AEF growth assumed 2%
findings.quote: Following WG's commitment that registered carers in Wales should receive the RLW, the MTFP includes RLW increases as among the factors likely to impact the future annual cost of commissioned care. The annual price increases factored into the MTFP for commissioned care are higher than anticipated AEF increases over the medium term and therefore represent an unfunded pressure.

findings.headline: School balances forecast to move into cumulative deficit of £2.4 million by March 2027, with recovery uncertain
findings.detail: The document forecasts aggregate school balances swinging from £0.4m surplus (March 2026) to £2.4m deficit by March 2027, driven by persistent cost pressures. The clear aim is to stop the deficit increasing further, with recovery not expected until 2028/29. The council notes this represents a financial resilience risk and requires temporary use of earmarked reserves not needed until 2029/30.
findings.matters: School deficits erode general fund resilience and signal service-level cash stress. The need to use reserves to cover school deficits reduces the council's buffer against other shocks.
findings.figures: School surplus March 2026: £0.4m; forecast deficit March 2027: £2.4m; cumulative reduction of £32m in school balances since March 2022
findings.quote: Current forecasts indicate that the aggregate surplus balance at the end of March 2026 is likely to be circa £0.4 million, compared to the forecast cumulative deficit for March 2026 of £5.0 million as-at March 2025. Over the short to medium-term, there remain cost pressures in schools to the extent that there remains a likely forecast of school balances being reduced to a deficit level of circa £2.4 million by March 2027.

findings.headline: Cumulative budget gap of £167 million over four years with no agreed funding baseline beyond 2026/27
findings.detail: Welsh Government has not provided funding figures for 2027/28 onwards. The MTFP assumes 2% annual AEF growth as a planning assumption, but this is unconfirmed. Annual budget gaps range from £43.8m (2027/28) to £48.2m (2030/31). The absence of confirmed funding creates material risk to the council's financial resilience.
findings.matters: Lending decisions depend on predictable cash flows; a council planning without confirmed government funding and needing to find £167m in solutions over four years presents heightened refinancing risk.
findings.quote: In the absence of any indicatives, the MTFP is currently predicated upon the assumption of a 2% funding increase per annum, broadly aligned to CPI expectations. The fact that funding figures are based, by necessity, on assumptions at this stage represents a material risk to the Council's financial resilience.

findings.headline: Cumulative workforce reduction of 1,700+ FTE over ten years, with further 64.2 FTE cuts in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council has deleted over 1,700 FTE posts in the past decade outside schools. The 2026/27 budget proposes net reduction of 64.2 FTE (66.2 deleted, 2.0 created), including 17.3 voluntary redundancies and 34.6 vacant post deletions. The report states 'None of the proposals planned for 2026/27 have an adverse impact on service delivery' but given ongoing demand pressures in social care and education, capacity risk is material.
findings.matters: Large cumulative workforce reductions combined with rising demand in statutory services creates service delivery and quality risk. The claim that redundancies have 'no significant impact on resident/customer' is difficult to reconcile with £18m+ demand pressures.
findings.figures: 1,700+ FTE deleted over ten years; 394.43 FTE annual average reduction 2023-2026; 66.2 FTE deletion and 2.0 FTE creation in 2026/27, net 64.2 reduction
findings.quote: Over the past ten years budget proposals resulted in the reduction of over 1,700 FTE posts in services other than schools.

findings.headline: Persistent income underperformance in fees and charges across planning, building control, and venues
findings.detail: The 2025/26 monitoring shows ongoing income shortfalls, and realignments of £1.799m have been budgeted for 'underachieving income budgets in areas including planning and building control, City Hall functions, residential and nursing, and library fines'. The report delegates authority to officers to amend fees during the year 'where necessary in consultation with the Cabinet Member', suggesting income targets are uncertain.
findings.matters: Chronic underperformance against income targets indicates either overoptimistic budget setting or structural barriers (demand weakness, policy constraints) to raising revenue from fees. This is a red flag for budget control.
findings.figures: £1.799m income pressure realignment for 2026/27
findings.quote: Income pressures (£1.799 million) – underachieving income budgets in areas including planning and building control, City Hall functions, residential and nursing, and library fines.

findings.headline: Shared Prosperity Fund revenue reduction of £6.929 million with one-year funding certainty only
findings.detail: SPF funding drops from £10.136m (2025/26) to £3.207m (2026/27), a £6.929m revenue reduction. The 'transition' to a new Local Growth Fund is for one year only, with new arrangements and funding levels unknown for 2027/28 onwards. The budget includes £2.25m base budget allocation and temporary reserves use to mitigate, but this is described as a 'combination' of measures, not a permanent solution.
findings.matters: Single-year funding with uncertain renewal creates service continuity risk and forces reliance on temporary funding sources. When the transition year ends, the council will face similar pressures again.
findings.figures: £6.929m reduction in SPF revenue funding; £10.711m SPF allocation for 2026/27 (total, of which £3.207m revenue); £3.312m total fall compared to 2025/26
findings.quote: This mitigation more than doubles the amount that would otherwise be available through LGF alone in 2026/27. Whilst there will still inevitably be a degree of impact on services linked to the residual level of fall out, it is intended that this will be managed in a strategic way.

findings.headline: 2025/26 directorate overspend of £5.767 million despite month 9 containment, signalling ongoing service cost control difficulty
findings.detail: The current year (2025/26) shows a directorate-level overspend of £5.767m at month 9, driven by 'sustained demand pressure in Children's Services and Retained Education and income shortfalls within Planning Transport & Environment and Economic Development'. The report notes 'the directorate position will need further action over coming months' and has realigned the 2026/27 budget to absorb these ongoing issues.
findings.matters: A council unable to control current-year spending risks missing the 2026/27 balanced budget target and signals that cost pressures are embedded and difficult to manage. The realignment of 2026/27 budgets to accommodate 2025/26 overruns reduces flexibility.
findings.figures: £5.767m directorate overspend at month 9; offset partly by £4.550m underspend on capital financing and £1.0m on council tax collection
findings.quote: The overall monitoring position, as at Month 9, reflects a total projected net annual Council overspend of £0.217 million... the directorate position will need further action over coming months.

findings.headline: Demand pressures in social care and ALN consuming 70% of growth envelope, with over £10 million in pressures
findings.detail: Of the £18.03m demand pressures identified, over 70% relates to Additional Learning Needs (ALN) across special schools, transport and placements. Adult Services demands £3.135m and Children's Services £3.777m (including a £1.5m uplift to contingency). These are recurrent structural pressures, not one-off costs, and the report notes ALN 'growing pressure is a picture that is replicated over the medium-term'.
findings.matters: Persistent demand growth in statutory services (social care, education for children with additional needs) crowds out discretionary spending and indicates the council is managing increasing complexity with finite resources. This pattern typically continues or accelerates.
findings.figures: £18.030m total demand pressure; ALN over 70% of this; Adult Services £3.135m, Children's Services £3.777m
findings.quote: Over 70% of the £18.030 million demand pressure is linked to pressures in Additional Learning Needs; this growing pressure is a picture that is replicated over the medium-term.

findings.headline: Over £110 million in specific grants remain unconfirmed for 2026/27, creating cash flow uncertainty
findings.detail: Key grants totalling over £110m have not been confirmed, including Retail Leisure & Hospitality Rates Relief (£76.4m), Sustainable Waste Management (£16.4m), and others. The budget does not assume pEPR funding as a base allocation, and the report notes the SPF/Local Growth Fund arrangements are still being finalised and 'subject to an ongoing assessment process linked to performance against recycling targets'.
findings.matters: Unconfirmed grants create material cash flow and budget execution risk. If grants are delayed or reduced, the council lacks identified mitigation. The pEPR reduction from £10.1m to £6.1m shows how grant funding can fluctuate based on performance metrics outside the council's control.
findings.figures: £76.363m (Retail Leisure & Hospitality), £16.4m (Waste), £7.242m (LAEG Demand Led), £3.654m (VAWDASV), £2.959m (Period Dignity); pEPR reduced from £10.059m to £6.059m
findings.quote: Grants totalling more than £110 million are yet to be confirmed for 2026/27 including Retail, Leisure and Hospitality Rates Relief (£76.363 million)... This results in a risk to future grant awards which must be factored into spend plans for the service.

findings.headline: Core office scheme capital cost escalated to £111 million borrowing requirement, adding £33 million in financing costs
findings.detail: The Core Office project was budgeted at £80.3m in 2025/26 but revised forecasts now project £111m borrowing requirement. The £33m increase in capital financing costs has been captured in the MTFP, though the report notes 'it should be noted that this is considered a prudent estimate at this stage and the Directorate are reviewing various options to mitigate pressures and reduce costs accordingly', indicating further cost surprises are possible.
findings.matters: Project cost overruns of 38% on a major council asset scheme demonstrate capital governance and forecasting risk. The qualification that this is 'prudent' and costs are 'under review' suggests material downside scenarios exist.
findings.figures: £80.3m initial budget, £111m revised borrowing requirement, £33m additional capital financing costs
findings.quote: Updated forecasts are such that a borrowing requirement of £111 million is now estimated, which results in additional borrowing costs of £33 million.

findings.headline: School sector forecast to move from £0.4m surplus to £2.5m deficit by March 2027
findings.detail: Despite an improved near-term forecast, schools are projected to shift to a cumulative deficit within 12 months due to ALN pressures, pay awards and inflation. The report acknowledges 'there remains a likelihood that there will be a cumulative negative balance figure' and notes 'every effort will be made in partnership with schools to explore ways of avoiding this position, but education outcomes will be uppermost in the mind'.
findings.matters: School deficits indicate service demand outpacing available resources and signal the council's difficulty in managing pressures in statutory services. This is a leading indicator of broader financial stress.
findings.figures: £0.4m surplus forecast March 2026, declining to deficit of 'just under £2.5m by March 2027'
findings.quote: Looking forward to 2026/27 and the next two years, there remain cost pressures in schools to the extent that there remains a likely forecast of school balances being reduced to a deficit level of just under £2.5 million by March 2027.

findings.headline: Medium-term budget gap of £167 million projected across 2027/28 to 2030/31 with no defined solution strategy
findings.detail: The MTFP projects deficits of £43.8m in 2027/28, £34.9m in 2028/29, £40.2m in 2029/30, and £48.2m in 2030/31. The report states work on developing proposals 'will commence following approval of the 2026/27 Budget', meaning solutions remain unidentified and will rely on unspecified future service cuts or further tax increases.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in a council's ability to manage multi-year deficits. This projection shows structural pressures with solutions deferred, creating material refinancing risk.
findings.quote: Work on developing a fully defined set of proposals for the medium term, and in particular for 2027/28, will commence following approval of the 2026/27 Budget.

findings.headline: Homelessness pressures driving £1,166k reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The Homelessness reserve will fall from £2,428k to £1,262k as £1,166k is drawn down to manage rising homelessness costs. The reserve explicitly notes it is to manage increasing homelessness pressures.
findings.matters: Growing homelessness costs that require significant and ongoing reserve support indicate a structural demand pressure on the council budget.
findings.figures: £2,428k at 31.03.2026; (£1,166k) drawdown; £1,262k remaining
findings.quote: Homelessness 2,428 0 (1,166) 1,262 Increases in homelessness pressures

findings.headline: General Fund earmarked reserves reducing by £20,490k (16%) in one year
findings.detail: Total General Fund earmarked reserves forecast to fall from £128,330k to £107,840k. This 16% reduction in a single year represents significant depletion of the council's financial resilience buffer.
findings.matters: A large annual drawdown of reserves indicates ongoing budget pressures and reduces financial headroom for unexpected events.
findings.figures: £128,330k opening; £107,840k closing; £20,490k used

findings.headline: Adults Social Care reserve depleted 88%, falling to £264k
findings.detail: The Adults Social Care earmarked reserve will fall from £2,234k to £264k through a £1,970k drawdown to manage service-specific pressures. This leaves minimal reserves for a major, inherently volatile demand-driven service.
findings.matters: Adult social care typically faces unpredictable demand pressures; reserves this low leave the council vulnerable to unexpected costs.
findings.figures: £2,234k at 31.03.2026; (£1,970k) drawdown; £264k remaining
