findings.headline: Schools reserves will move into deficit of £2,438k in 2026/27
findings.detail: Schools aggregate reserves are forecast to move from £362k positive to £2,438k negative, requiring a £2,800k drawdown. This indicates structural school budget deficits that will need recovery plans.
findings.matters: Schools with deficits are a statutory concern for councils and indicate budget pressures in the education sector that the council must manage.
findings.quote: Schools Reserves 362 0 (2,800) (2,438) Aggregate School Balances / Deficits

findings.headline: New rent policy limits flexibility; any CPI outcome below 3% reduces rent uplift to CPI+1%, restricting resources and increasing risk to capital programme affordability.
findings.detail: A new 10-year Welsh Government Social Housing Rent Policy (from 1 April 2026) sets maximum annual increases based on CPI bands: 0-3% CPI = CPI+1%, 3-5% CPI = CPI+0.5%, >5% CPI = Welsh Ministers decide. The September 2025 CPI of 3.8% resulted in a 4.3% uplift for 2026-27, £585,000 above the 3.7% previously assumed. However, forward modelling assumes CPI+1% in future years (3.3% for 2027-28 down to 3.0% for 2030-31). The document flags: 'Any rent uplift lower than assumed would significantly impact on the available resources for the HRA and is therefore a risk to future resilience.'
findings.matters: Rent income is the only controllable lever in the budget. A policy framework that limits uplifts based on CPI bands constrains the council's ability to respond to cost inflation. If inflation falls, rent uplifts fall further, widening the budget gap and forcing earlier reserve depletion.
findings.figures: 2026-27 uplift 4.3%; forward assumptions 3.3% (2027-28), 3.0% (2028-29), 3.1% (2029-30), 3.0% (2030-31); sensitivity shows 1% CPI reduction = £485k income loss
findings.quote: Any rent uplift lower than assumed would significantly impact on the available resources for the HRA and is therefore a risk to future resilience. This requires consideration of mitigation opportunities including efficiencies, service change and prioritisation and potentially a consideration of affordability in respect of the new build programme.

findings.headline: Interest rate exposure is significant and modelled assumptions are already exceeded; a 1% rise in rates costs £5.263 million per year.
findings.detail: Capital financing is modelled at 4.25% interest payable. However, PWLB rates are currently 'over 6%, above assumptions in viability modelling.' This means actual borrowing costs are already higher than the budget assumes. The sensitivity analysis shows that a 1% increase in interest rates from the modelled 4.25% to 5.25% would cost £5.263 million in 2026-27. The council flags this as reducing 'future affordability for borrowing-dependent activity.'
findings.matters: The council is exposed to interest rate movements on a growing debt burden (CFR at 4.57x revenue stream in 2026-27). Current PWLB rates are already 175 basis points above budget assumption, creating an immediate affordability shortfall that is not fully reflected in the numbers.
findings.figures: Modelled interest rate 4.25%; current PWLB rates over 6%; 1% rate increase costs £5.263m annually; CFR £580.9m (estimated from tables) at 4.57x the net revenue stream of £124.206m
findings.quote: PWLB rates remain elevated (over 6%), above assumptions in viability modelling. Higher rates reduce future affordability for borrowing-dependent activity and underline the need for prompt grant claims.

findings.headline: Service quality investment of £2.8 million in 2026-27 signals existing service delivery is under pressure; responsive repairs complaints and backlogs remain unresolved.
findings.detail: The council is investing £2.8 million in 2026-27 to strengthen core service provision, with £1.7 million expanding the Responsive Repairs Unit and £1.1 million adding housing management and anti-social behaviour posts. This follows tenant satisfaction survey results showing 'ongoing challenges remain in key operational areas, particularly complaint handling, responsive repairs, and communication between tenants and the antisocial behaviour team.' The investment is described as addressing 'frontline functions to ensure tenants continue to receive a good quality service.'
findings.matters: Tenant satisfaction is weak and the council is forced to invest additional revenue to maintain basic service levels. This diverts resources from other priorities and suggests demand for repairs and support exceeds current capacity, increasing financial pressure.
findings.figures: £2.8m investment in 2026-27 for core services; £1.7m for responsive repairs expansion; £1.1m for housing management posts
findings.quote: Although significant work has been undertaken to strengthen service delivery, service area data and the Tenant Satisfaction Survey results for 2025/26 indicate that ongoing challenges remain in key operational areas, particularly complaint handling, responsive repairs, and communication between tenants and the antisocial behaviour team.

findings.headline: Employers' National Insurance costs of £800,000 in 2026-27 are unfunded; Welsh Government has confirmed no external support will be provided.
findings.detail: The budget now includes all National Insurance employers' costs as it has been confirmed that no external funding will be made available. This represents an additional budget impact of £800,000 for 2026-27 and will continue to affect future years.
findings.matters: This is an unexpected cost pressure that the council must absorb from existing revenue. It represents an avoidable hit to the budget gap and demonstrates limited flexibility to absorb cost pressures from outside the HRA.
findings.figures: £800,000 additional budget impact for 2026-27; confirmed as unfunded
findings.quote: In terms of National Insurance employers' increased costs, it should be noted that the budget and MTFP now includes all costs as it has been confirmed that no external funding will be made available. This is an additional budget impact of circa £800,000 for 2026-27.

findings.headline: Welsh Government grant funding for capital schemes is neither secured nor reliable; timing is inconsistent and the council flags this as creating cost and uncertainty.
findings.detail: The capital investment programme has a 'clear reliance on significant additional and sustained grant funding subsidy for projects. Without this they are neither affordable nor deliverable in the timescales set out. Such funding is not secured.' The risk matrix notes that timing of WG grant approvals and payments 'remains inconsistent, creating cost and uncertainty for the Council', with issues stemming from technical approval processes and year-end delays. Extended timescales have recently been agreed for some schemes, but uncertainty remains.
findings.matters: The council cannot proceed with capital schemes unless grant is confirmed, yet grant decisions are subject to WG process delays and are not guaranteed. This creates capital programme uncertainty and risk of abortive costs. Any reduction in WG funding would force reprioritisation or programme deferral.
findings.figures: External grant and contributions estimated at £331.794m over five years (44.9% of £739.455m total capital expenditure); Social Housing Grant and Transitional Accommodation grant assumed but 'usually only available on an annual bid process'
findings.quote: The capital expenditure commitments for the HRA incurred previously and proposed for the future in the budget have a clear reliance on significant additional and sustained grant funding subsidy for projects. Without this they are neither affordable nor deliverable in the timescales set out. Such funding is not secured.

findings.headline: New build programme has slipped, losing £835,000 in rental income and creating holding costs; new build risk is rated Red and remains critical to medium-term viability.
findings.detail: Changes to stock levels due to slippage of new build schemes, meanwhile use, and reductions in units (e.g. Tyndall Court) have created a net reduction in rental and service charge income of £835,000 for 2026-27. The risk matrix rates failure to meet new build targets as 'Red', with impacts including delayed housing need reduction, increased temporary accommodation costs, holding costs of vacant sites, and reduced rental income. Stock completions are essential to offset capital financing costs from 2031-32 onwards.
findings.matters: The council's medium-term financial model assumes the new build programme will remove the budget gap from 2031-32 onwards by delivering rental income that covers increased capital financing costs. Slippage delays this transition and extends reserve drawdowns. Further delays could make the long-term position unviable.
findings.figures: £835,000 net reduction in rental and service charge income for 2026-27 due to stock slippage; stock numbers declining 14,450 (2026-27) to ultimately 16,085 (2030-31); new build programme scale £571.910m capital over five years
findings.quote: The increase in rental income for standard and community living stock as a result of the higher CPI for 2026/27 is impacted by other changes to key assumptions around stock linked to overall rent levels. These include changes to stock levels as a result of slippage of new build schemes.

findings.headline: Decarbonisation to meet Welsh Housing Quality Standards 2023 is unfunded and mandatory; costs of £351m (SAP 75 by 2030) to £866m (EPC A) are not budgeted.
findings.detail: The council has submitted a compliance policy to Welsh Government outlining projected decarbonisation costs. Current budget includes only costs of existing requirements and early pilot schemes funded separately. No amount has been included for the financial impact of meeting WHQS 23 decarbonisation targets. The risk matrix rates this as 'Red': 'Without additional funding, the cost of meeting requirements would displace other capital priorities and create significant unfunded revenue pressures, risking the overall viability of the HRA Business Plan.'
findings.matters: This is a known, quantified, statutory obligation with no identified funding source. If Welsh Government does not provide substantial grant support, the council faces either non-compliance (regulatory risk) or a major unplanned capital draw that will further strain the budget gap and reserves.
findings.figures: SAP 75 by 2030: £351m for 99.8% of stock; SAP A (EPC 92): £866m; incremental cost £515m for the remaining properties
findings.quote: Achieving SAP 75 is estimated to cost £351m (applicable to 99.8% of homes). Reaching SAP 92 (EPC A) would cost £866m, requiring an additional £515m and achievable for around 19% of stock. Significant external funding and technological advances will be needed to meet these targets.

findings.headline: Only £85,000 of £4.16 million in claimed five-year efficiencies has been identified for 2026-27; the remainder are aspirational.
findings.detail: The council identified only £85,000 in achievable cost efficiencies for 2026-27 (digital technologies £15k, grant funding £64k, accommodation restructure £6k). It proposes to develop a 'detailed five-year efficiencies plan' for 2027-28 onwards claiming £4.16 million across five years, but acknowledges 'very limited options for cost efficiencies during 2026/27' due to service pressures.
findings.matters: The gap between claimed and delivered savings is a warning signal. The efficiencies plan is not costed, not committed to, and depends on future 'detailed review'. If the £4.16m does not materialise, the budget gap widens and reserve depletion accelerates.
findings.figures: 2026-27 efficiencies £85,000; claimed five-year programme £4.16m; budget gap £10.62m over MTFP after the claimed savings are assumed
findings.quote: Due to the pressures on the service, there were very limited options for cost efficiencies during 2026/27 as outlined in the table below.

findings.headline: Capital financing costs are growing to 37.65% of net revenue by 2032-33, described as an 'unprecedented expansion' of borrowing that cannot be reversed.
findings.detail: Capital financing costs rise from 29.18% of net revenue in 2024-25 to 32.46% in 2026-27 and 37.65% by 2032-33. The Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) ratio climbs to 5.10x the net revenue stream by 2029-30. The council flags this explicitly as an unprecedented commitment that cannot be reversed, requiring robust viability assessment and scrutiny.
findings.matters: This leverage trajectory is aggressive and constrains the council's future flexibility. At 37.65% of revenue dedicated to capital financing, any adverse movement in interest rates or rental income severely impacts service delivery. Lenders need to understand whether this is sustainable.
findings.figures: Capital financing 29.18% of revenue (2024-25 actual) to 37.65% (2032-33 est); CFR ratio 3.96x (2024-25) to 5.10x (2029-30)
findings.quote: This represents an unprecedented expansion of the Capital Financing Requirement and consequential impact on the revenue budget. Entering into commitments for borrowing cannot be reversed.

findings.headline: A £10.62 million budget gap over the medium term will be met by drawing down reserves from £23.7m to £13.1m.
findings.detail: The updated MTFP continues to indicate a temporary budget gap of £10.62 million over the period, after £4.16 million in assumed efficiency savings. The council plans to offset the residual budget gap with earmarked reserves. This leaves closing reserves of £13.077 million at the end of the MTFP period, down from an opening balance of £23.694 million.
findings.matters: Declining reserves limit the council's ability to absorb shocks and signal tightening financial headroom. A lender needs to know whether this trajectory is sustainable or whether further pressures could render the HRA unviable.
findings.figures: Opening reserves £23.694m, closing reserves £13.077m, budget gap £10.62m over MTFP, only £1.133m drawdown in 2026/27 but rising to £3.4m in 2028/29
findings.quote: The updated 2026/27 budget and MTFP set out in this Annex continues to indicate a temporary budget gap, estimated at £10.62 million over the MTFP period, after assuming targeted efficiency savings and service change estimated at £4.16 million over the MTFP period.

findings.headline: Invest to Save schemes assumed net-neutral to revenue budget but carry significant delivery risk if savings do not materialize
findings.detail: The council is proposing £177.672m of borrowing for Invest to Save schemes over five years, assuming these will be repaid from realized savings or incidental income. The strategy acknowledges: 'Although there may be short term implications, Invest to Save schemes are intended to be net neutral on the capital financing budget. However, there are risks that the level of incidental income, savings or capital receipts anticipated from such schemes will be delayed or will not materialise. This would have a detrimental long-term consequence on the revenue budget.' The gross capital financing ratio (8.47%) reflects this worst-case scenario where savings do not land.
findings.matters: £177.7m of borrowing is contingent on realization of savings that may not occur; if even 50% of assumed savings fail to materialize, revenue budget impact jumps from net-neutral to circa £2-3m ongoing commitment
findings.figures: Invest to Save borrowing: £177.672m total; largest schemes vehicles (£23.075m), Joint Equipment Store (£8.399m), Refit 4 property efficiency (£4.985m)
findings.quote: Although there may be short term implications, Invest to Save schemes are intended to be net neutral on the capital financing budget. However, there are risks that the level of incidental income, savings or capital receipts anticipated from such schemes will be delayed or will not materialise. This would have a detrimental long-term consequence on the revenue budget and requires careful monitoring when considering future levels of additional borrowing.

findings.headline: Grant funding volatility creates medium-term planning uncertainty: £78m of 2026/27 capital program subject to bid approval and short-term awards
findings.detail: £78.067m (21.3%) of the 2026/27 General Fund capital programme is assumed to come from external grants and contributions, almost entirely from Welsh Government on a competitive bidding basis. The strategy explicitly notes: 'The short-term nature of grant awards makes long term planning and delivery of strategic schemes extremely difficult.' This creates recurring execution risk and forces the council to maintain a 'pipeline of projects' hoping to attract funding when it becomes available.
findings.matters: One-fifth of the capital programme is contingent on grant approvals outside council control; any grant withdrawal or bidding failure requires immediate borrowing substitution or programme deferral
findings.figures: External grants and contributions: £78.067m (2026/27); £228.333m over five years; 31% of total programme funding
findings.quote: The short-term nature of grant awards makes long term planning and delivery of strategic schemes extremely difficult. Where external grant funding bids are made, it is essential that these are in line with Council priorities and include consideration of any revenue budget consequences.

findings.headline: Asset disposals and rationalization explicitly required to support affordability of future capital investment needs
findings.detail: The strategy states that 'the approach to progressing, rationalisation and disposal of all assets is essential to support the costs of capital investment and to minimise maintenance liabilities.' This is not a discretionary efficiency opportunity but a stated requirement to make the capital programme affordable. The council recognizes it 'cannot afford to do everything' and further activity 'may need to be paused' or 'spread over a longer period'.
findings.matters: Explicit requirement for asset sales to fund capital programme indicates the council cannot grow investment from revenue alone; forces choice between asset base reduction and capital investment cessation
findings.figures: No specific disposal targets or timings quantified for future years beyond current shortfall
findings.quote: The approach to progressing, rationalisation and disposal of all assets is essential to support the costs of capital investment and to minimise maintenance liabilities.

findings.headline: HRA capital financing costs will reach 37.48% of housing revenue by 2030/31 — structurally unsustainable debt burden
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account (HRA) capital financing costs will consume 37.48% of the HRA's revenue stream by 2030/31, rising from 29.18% in 2024/25. HRA debt itself will grow from £421m to £754m over the same period. The strategy explicitly warns: 'No control over rent policy, new housing standards, revenue cost pressures, grant uncertainty are major factors impacting on wider Council financial resilience risk.' At 37.48%, the HRA is allocating more than one-third of its entire revenue to repaying capital, leaving minimal space for maintenance, management, or service delivery.
findings.matters: HRA financing ratios above 35% indicate a housing programme that cannot be sustained from rental income alone; any rent policy constraint or cost pressure will force asset sales or service cuts
findings.quote: Housing Revenue Account – Investment is increasing significantly over the long term. No control over rent policy, new housing standards, revenue cost pressures, grant uncertainty are major factors impacting on wider Council financial resilience risk.

findings.headline: Capital financing costs rising to 8.47% of General Fund revenue budget by 2030/31 (gross ratio), limiting fiscal headroom
findings.detail: The gross capital financing cost ratio for the General Fund will reach 8.47% by 2030/31, up from 6.65% in 2024/25. This means nearly 8.5p of every pound of revenue budget is committed to repaying capital expenditure, before any efficiency savings or service cost pressures. The net ratio reaches 5.13% despite assuming Invest to Save schemes will be self-funding, indicating material downside risk.
findings.matters: High capital financing ratios constrain council's ability to invest in services, respond to demand pressures, or absorb unexpected costs; the rising trend indicates deteriorating financial position
findings.figures: General Fund gross capital financing ratio: 6.65% (2024/25) → 8.47% (2030/31); net ratio: 4.07% → 5.13%
findings.quote: The percentage of the Council's revenue budget that is committed in the long term to capital financing costs is increasing. Given the pressure on revenue budgets, this limits the affordability of other priorities in future years and must be a factor considered by members when determining the Capital Programme

findings.headline: The arena construction is funded by the Council on 45-year repayment from operator income and car park income, creating long-term revenue dependency risk.
findings.detail: A Cabinet-approved funding strategy from November 2023 commits the Council to directly fund arena construction, with the costs 'intended to be met over a 45-year period from operator income and car park income receivable.' The Council notes 'the optimal funding solution is for the Council to provide the funding to construct the arena,' increasing the CFR. This embeds a 45-year bet on the commercial operator's performance and car park revenues, both outside the Council's direct control.
findings.matters: Long-term debt service that depends on third-party commercial performance creates a tail risk. If operator returns or car park income miss forecasts, the Council must cover the shortfall from general revenues.
findings.figures: Arena funding term: 45 years; funding sources: operator income and car park income
findings.quote: Council contribution to the enabling costs and multi storey car parking for the arena and also to 'Direct Fund' the Arena construction following the approval by Cabinet in November 2023 of a funding strategy. The optimal funding solution is for the Council to provide the funding to construct the arena. Whilst this will increase the Council's Capital Financing Requirement and need to borrow, the costs of the solution are intended to be met over a 45-year period from operator income and car park income receivable.

findings.headline: £18 million of LOBO loans face forced refinancing on 21 May 2026, when lenders can reset rates every six months at current elevated interest rates.
findings.detail: Cardiff holds four LOBO loans totalling £23 million. On three of these (£18 million total), the lender can request a rate change every six months; the next opportunity is 21/05/2026. The document states 'given current interest rates, the likelihood of a change in rate is elevated, at which point the Council would aim to refinance loans.' At 4.06%–4.35% today, refinancing at higher rates would increase annual interest costs.
findings.matters: A lender wants to know whether the Council can absorb a sudden repricing of debt or forced refinancing at unfavourable rates. LOBO calls are a known pressure point in the coming months.
findings.figures: Four LOBO loans totalling £23m; £18m subject to six-monthly rate resets; £5m subject to five-yearly call; existing rates 4.06%–4.35%
findings.quote: Given current interest rates, the likelihood of a change in rate is elevated, at which point the Council would aim to refinance loans. It should be noted that £18 million of the LOBO loans are currently subject to the lender potentially requesting a change in the rate of interest payable every six months.

findings.headline: The Council faces a £928 million borrowing shortfall by 2030/31, with internal cash insufficient to cover planned capital investment.
findings.detail: The capital financing requirement is projected to reach £1,697 million by 2030/31, but external borrowing is planned at only £769 million after repayments. This £928 million gap—55% of the CFR—means the Council must undertake substantial further external borrowing in future years. The document notes this arises from 'an ambitious capital investment programme which almost doubles the size of the existing borrowing.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the Council can service nearly £1 billion of additional debt, and how it will be staged and funded. This is the structural financing question for the next five years.
findings.figures: CFR 2030/31: £1,697m; External borrowing 2030/31: £769m; Shortfall: £928m (55% of CFR)
findings.quote: The difference between the projected CFR in 2030/31 (£1,697 million) and the actual level of external borrowing after any planned repayments (£769 million) is £928 million, i.e. there is insufficient cash held by the Council to support this projected level of under borrowing and this means there is a requirement for the Council to undertake further external borrowing in future years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7(b) Financial Resilience Risk and Mitigations
findings.headline: Cardiff faces a £167 million budget gap from 2027/28 to 2030/31
findings.detail: The council has identified a structural budget gap of £167 million across the medium-term financial planning period. This is the stated context for all the financial resilience risks documented in this appendix.
findings.matters: A four-year budget gap of this scale indicates fundamental structural pressure on the council's finances that will require either substantial service reductions, additional income, or draw-down from reserves — all material to lenders' assessments.
findings.figures: £167 million for the period 2027/28 to 2030/31
findings.quote: Within the context of there being a Budget Gap of £167 million for the period 2027/28 to 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: 2025-12-18 Rent Setting Appendix E - Rent Setting Consultation
findings.headline: Majority support maximum Welsh Government rents contingent on affordability
findings.detail: 65.7% of respondents agreed with setting rents at the full amount allowed by Welsh Government, conditional on demonstrating affordability and value for money.
findings.matters: Tenant acceptance of maximum rents reduces political resistance and potential arrears backlash, but council must credibly protect affordability for the 25.6% already struggling to pay
findings.quote: Do you agree with the proposal to set rents in line with the full amount allowed by the Welsh Government, as long as this is affordable? Yes No (Base: 324)

findings.paper_title: 2025-12-18 Rent Setting Appendix E - Rent Setting Consultation
findings.headline: 25.6% of tenants report current difficulties paying rent
findings.detail: Of 328 respondents to the October 2025 consultation, 25.6% reported currently experiencing difficulties paying rent. This represents material payment stress within the current tenant population at existing rent levels.
findings.matters: Current rent payment difficulties directly signal arrears risk and HRA income volatility; any further rent increase will worsen affordability for an already-stressed cohort
findings.quote: Are you currently experiencing any difficulties in paying your rent? Yes No (Base: 328)

findings.headline: Significant risks to HRA financial resilience requiring close monitoring and potential impact on service delivery and capital investment
findings.detail: The paper explicitly identifies 'a number of significant risks to the financial resilience of the HRA which will need to be monitored and managed closely.' It notes that 'Where a budget shortfall cannot be mitigated by other offsets, it will have the potential to impact on the level and quality of service provision to tenants and on the capital schemes that can be taken forward.' The document acknowledges uncontrollable variables including rent levels, interest rates, and construction inflation.
findings.matters: An explicit governance-level acknowledgment of financial resilience risk is a red flag. It indicates the council recognises that the HRA is operating at or beyond its capacity to absorb cost shocks without materially impacting service or investment. This limits the council's strategic flexibility.
findings.figures: Council will need to 'review and prioritise revenue operating costs' and conduct 'review and reprioritisation of the HRA Capital Programme'
findings.quote: There are a number of significant risks to the financial resilience of the HRA which will need to be monitored and managed closely.

findings.headline: Interest rate and borrowing cost pressures on ambitious new build programme
findings.detail: The paper lists 'Increase in interest rates on new borrowing' as a key HRA pressure and notes increased borrowing requirement to fund new homes. It acknowledges 'significant capital expenditure commitments for the HRA both incurred and proposed for the future, with a resultant increased borrowing requirement.' However, capital financing costs fell £1 million in 2026/27 only because of 'delay in the timing of payments and delivery of planned and new build projects to future years', masking underlying pressure.
findings.matters: Rising interest rates on HRA borrowing increase annual servicing costs and reduce the funding available for maintenance and services. If the council is deferring projects to manage cash, it signals that the borrowing programme may not be sustainably priced into the business plan.
findings.figures: £1 million reduction in capital financing costs is due to project delays, not reduced borrowing
findings.quote: The capital financing costs estimate has reduced by an estimated £1 million, reflecting a delay in the timing of payments and delivery of planned and new build projects to future years compared to the initial assumptions when the capital programme was approved.

findings.headline: Rent recovery deteriorating due to cost of living and Universal Credit migration
findings.detail: The paper identifies 'Rent recovery levels due to ongoing cost of living issues and migration to Universal Credit' as a key HRA pressure. Separately, 25.6% of surveyed tenants reported difficulty paying rent, and the paper notes ongoing high arrears demand requiring dedicated support teams.
findings.matters: Falling rent collection is an early warning of tenant financial stress that foreshadows either write-offs (bad debt) or unsustainable arrears requiring service intervention. Universal Credit migration often creates collection gaps because of payment delays and underpayment of housing costs.
findings.figures: 88.74% of tenants in receipt of benefits; 25.6% of surveyed tenants experiencing rent payment difficulties
findings.quote: Rent recovery levels due to ongoing cost of living issues and migration to Universal Credit

findings.headline: Staffing costs rising by £1.622 million including impact of National Insurance pressures
findings.detail: Staffing costs are increasing by £1.622 million for 2026/27, driven by revised establishment levels, pay progression, forecast pay awards, and 'the impact of National Insurance pressures'. This is a significant fixed cost that will not flex with service demand.
findings.matters: Staffing is often the largest controllable cost in housing revenue accounts. Rising staffing costs that outpace income growth indicate either service expansion under financial duress or inability to right-size the establishment to match affordable service levels.
findings.figures: £1.622 million additional staffing funding requirement
findings.quote: The staffing cost estimate reflects a revised 2026/27 establishment and related funding requirement (inclusive of incremental pay progression and the impact of National Insurance pressures) and uplifted for the 2025/26 pay award and the forecast pay award for 2026/27. This additional funding requirement is estimated at £1.622 million.

findings.headline: Housing Repairs Account funding requirement increasing by £1.778 million due to backlog and new contract costs
findings.detail: The Housing Repairs Account (maintenance and responsive repairs) requires an additional £1.778 million in funding for 2026/27. This is driven by management of a works backlog and costs of new contracts effective from January 2026. The paper lists 'ongoing demand on Responsive Repairs, especially for damp and mould cases' as a key pressure, suggesting reactive rather than preventative spend.
findings.matters: Rising maintenance costs that aren't being met by current income indicate deteriorating stock condition or deferred maintenance catching up. This is a pressure that compounds annually and can signal wider asset management problems.
findings.figures: £1.778 million additional requirement
findings.quote: The Housing Repairs Account funding requirement is anticipated to increase by £1.778 million to address the additional demands on the service; the management of a works backlog and to provide for costs of the new contracts due to be effective from January 2026.

findings.headline: £2.5m HRA budget shortfall even with maximum 4.3% rent increase proposed
findings.detail: Even applying the full Welsh Government-allowed rent increase of 4.3%, Cardiff Council faces a provisional revenue budget shortfall of £2.5 million for 2026/27. Service charge increases reduce this to £1.7 million, but the paper explicitly states 'it is clear that any savings available will not be sufficient to offset the increasing financial pressures' and the shortfall will need to be addressed 'with use of reserves to balance the budget in the short term.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether a council can sustain its borrowing and operations without continuously drawing down reserves. Reserve depletion is a one-off fix that cannot address ongoing structural deficits, limiting financial resilience and future investment capacity.
findings.figures: £2.5 million budget shortfall reduced to £1.7 million; only £96,000 in efficiency savings identified to date
findings.quote: Preliminary modelling indicates a potential revenue budget shortfall of circa £2.5 million for 2026/27, based on estimated cost pressures and information at this time.

findings.paper_title: 2025-12-18 Rent Setting Appendix D - Single Impact Assessment
findings.headline: One quarter of surveyed tenants report payment difficulties, signalling affordability stress despite benefit support
findings.detail: Although 88.74% of council tenants receive housing benefits that largely cover rent increases, 25.6% of surveyed tenants reported experiencing payment difficulties. This indicates that benefit passthrough, while protective for the majority, does not eliminate arrears risk. Further rent increases could worsen collection rates for the 12% not receiving benefits.
findings.matters: Tenant payment difficulties translate directly to arrears risk and cash collection vulnerability. Rising payment difficulties combined with higher rent requirements could reduce collection rates and worsen the HRA cash position.
findings.figures: 88.74% of tenants in receipt of housing benefits; 25.6% of surveyed tenants experiencing payment difficulties; 74.4% reporting no difficulties
findings.quote: 74.4% tenants stated that they were not experiencing any difficulties in paying their rent, while 25.6% said that they were.

findings.paper_title: 2025-12-18 Rent Setting Appendix D - Single Impact Assessment
findings.headline: Community Living and specialist accommodation costs are escalating faster than current service charges can cover
findings.detail: The document identifies that Community Living schemes incur higher operating costs from enhanced staffing that are not fully offset by existing service charges. Homeless accommodation likewise requires service charge increases to £30/week to reflect actual operating costs. These cost escalations indicate structural pressure in specialist services that may worsen if demand continues to rise.
findings.matters: Specialist accommodation cost growth outpacing revenue increases creates emerging medium-term financial risk. With homelessness extended beyond historical norms, if demand does not fall as projected, the HRA deficit will deepen.
findings.figures: Community Living service charge increases capped at £10/week (excluding utilities); homeless accommodation up to £30/week maximum
findings.quote: Community Living accommodation continues to incur higher operating costs, primarily as a result of enhanced staffing requirements necessary to maintain the quality of service and support for residents. These costs are not fully met by the current level of service charges.

findings.paper_title: 2025-12-18 Rent Setting Appendix D - Single Impact Assessment
findings.headline: Cardiff's Housing Revenue Account faces a budget deficit being addressed through rent and service charge increases up to 4.3%
findings.detail: The council proposes to increase rents at the Welsh Government maximum (4.3% for 2026/27) and raise service charges on council homes to address a budget deficit in its HRA. The strategy relies on both income increases and cost efficiencies. Most tenants are benefits-supported, but the underlying financial imbalance between HRA costs and revenues remains.
findings.matters: An HRA deficit requiring structural income increases signals the council's housing service is consuming more resources than its revenue base supports. This directly affects council creditworthiness and medium-term borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: 4.3% maximum rent increase; service charge increases of £0.32–£0.78/week for houses, £0.32–£2.07/week for flats, £1.47–£30.00/week for homeless accommodation
findings.quote: The report will also brief Cabinet on how efficiencies will be made to address the budget deficit in the Housing Revenue Account

findings.headline: Energy efficiency savings claimed for new builds remain unproven and uncertain
findings.detail: The committee raised concerns about whether savings projected from energy efficiency improvements would actually be realised. Officers stated only that they would continue to monitor the outcome, offering no commitment to the forecast savings.
findings.matters: Unproven planned savings are a budget risk if they do not materialise; the council's inability to commit to forecast savings indicates uncertainty in its financial projections.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: Committee highlighted the increase with new builds, and raised concerns on if the savings suggested would be made (based on energy efficiency). Officers stated that they will continue to monitor this.

findings.headline: £1.8 million housing repairs funding consumed entirely by cost inflation, with no expansion of repair capacity
findings.detail: Despite receiving £1.8 million in additional funding, the council clarified that this covers rising unit costs of repairs, not an increase in the number of repairs completed. Officers stated the allocation goes to cost inflation rather than service expansion.
findings.matters: Cost inflation eroding entire budget allocations without expanding service output signals sustained cost pressure; the council cannot improve housing maintenance despite additional funding.
findings.figures: £1.8 million
findings.quote: the increase is to cover the increase of cost in completing the repairs, as opposed to the number of repairs completed

findings.headline: Homeless accommodation scheme costs exceeded initial estimates, driving a rent increase from £1.37 to £30
findings.detail: The council increased charges for homeless residents because new schemes' costs were higher than initially estimated. Officers confirmed this as the reason for raising the charge up to £30 per week. The committee sought clarity on this cost overrun.
findings.matters: Cost overruns on housing services indicate budget planning gaps or unexpected price inflation in service delivery; the inability to forecast accommodation costs accurately signals cost pressure risk.
findings.quote: it was increased up to £30, as a new schemes' costs were higher than first estimated

findings.paper_title: 2025-12-18 Rent Setting Appendix A - Current Pressures on the Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: 1,692 people in temporary accommodation; ambitious new-build programme requires substantial short-term capital funding
findings.detail: As of November 2025, Cardiff has 1,692 people in temporary accommodation (597 families, 847 single people, 248 young people). The council declared a Housing Emergency in December 2023 and is pursuing an ambitious new-build programme. While future rents will eventually repay borrowing, the council requires substantial capital funds in the short term.
findings.matters: The new-build programme requires substantial near-term capital borrowing, increasing debt levels and reducing cash available for other pressures.
findings.figures: 1,692 people in temporary accommodation; Housing Emergency declared December 2023
findings.quote: However, in the short term it is important that funds are available within the HRA to fund this capital investment.

findings.paper_title: 2025-12-18 Rent Setting Appendix A - Current Pressures on the Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Welsh Housing Quality Standard 2023 requires substantial capital investment by 2030–2034; grant amount remains to be confirmed
findings.detail: WHQS 2023 requires all council homes to reach EPC 'C' by 2030 and EPC 'A' by 2034, with full stock assessment due March 2027. The council has inspected 39.8% of properties using a new asset database system. Implementation costs are described as 'substantial', but the council has confirmed only partial grant funding, with the precise amount still to be determined.
findings.matters: Large capital requirement with uncertain grant funding creates significant HRA budget pressure and may force additional borrowing or reserves depletion.
findings.figures: 39.8% of properties inspected; March 2027 assessment deadline; EPC 'C' by 2030; EPC 'A' by 2034; costs 'substantial' but grant amount unconfirmed
findings.quote: The estimated costs associated with implementing the standard are substantial. While some additional grant funding has been confirmed for the delivery of WHQS 2023, the precise amount remains to be determined.

findings.paper_title: 2025-12-18 Rent Setting Appendix A - Current Pressures on the Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Electrical safety compliance at 95%; remaining 5% in legal proceedings for access, requiring additional resources
findings.detail: Electrical safety compliance improved from 90% to 95% through increased resources and additional contractors. The remaining 5% of non-compliant properties are in legal access proceedings, placing considerable pressure on the Tenancy Management Team. The council identifies additional resources as necessary to resolve access issues.
findings.matters: Electrical safety compliance is a statutory obligation; non-compliance creates liability and reputational risk.
findings.figures: Compliance increased from 90% to 95%; remaining 5% in legal proceedings
findings.quote: there has been an increase in compliance from 90% to 95% for electrical testing and this is continuing to rise. Most of those tests that are not complete are going through the legal process to gain access, this has put considerable pressure on the Tenancy Management Team, and additional resources will be required to address no access issues.

findings.paper_title: 2025-12-18 Rent Setting Appendix A - Current Pressures on the Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Repair backlog of 422 units; council planning to invest in workforce expansion to reduce expensive external contractor reliance
findings.detail: The council has 422 responsive repairs awaiting scheduling due to limited internal capacity. Although improved from previous levels, the council has relied on costly external contractors to clear the backlog. The council states repair costs are substantially lower with internal staff and is planning workforce expansion in 2026/27 to reduce contractor dependency and improve response times.
findings.matters: High contractor costs create immediate budget pressure; the workforce investment signals planned operational spending affecting HRA budget.
findings.figures: 422 repairs backlogged; internal repair costs substantially lower than contractor costs
findings.quote: Additional funding is required for 2026/27 to address the volume of outstanding repairs, shorten completion times, and decrease reliance on external contractors.

findings.paper_title: 2025-12-18 Rent Setting Appendix A - Current Pressures on the Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Borrowing costs in the HRA have increased substantially; interest rate risk and grant funding timing require active management
findings.detail: The council's HRA borrowing has increased significantly to fund the house building and stock investment programmes. The paper states the council must manage the level and timing of capital investment given interest rate risks and availability/timing of Welsh Government grant support. Material costs, contractor costs, and energy costs are also rising and need close monitoring.
findings.matters: Higher borrowing costs and forward interest rate exposure directly impact the HRA's cash flow and debt sustainability.
findings.figures: Borrowing costs described as 'substantial' with increases 'over the last few years'
findings.quote: Borrowing costs within the HRA are substantial and increases over the last few years are linked in the main to the successful delivery of the Directorate's house building programme as well as investment in the existing stock.

findings.headline: Additional Council Tax revenue from increased base may be offset by reduction in Welsh Government Revenue Support Grant
findings.detail: Council explicitly states that it will wait until the final Welsh Government financial settlement before claiming benefits from the £4.7m tax base increase, because 'if the Council Tax Base increases relative to the tax base of other councils, then Revenue Support Grant will reduce as a direct consequence'. The additional £4.7m projected for 2026/27 may not translate to net additional revenue.
findings.matters: The headline benefit of tax base growth (£4.7m additional revenue) is contingent on grant distribution outcomes outside the council's control, creating material revenue forecasting uncertainty.
findings.figures: £4,743,965 estimated additional revenue from tax base increase; Cardiff Council receives £3,809,407
findings.quote: Established practice is to wait until the final financial settlement from Welsh Government before taking any benefits from increased Council Tax Base. This is due to the fact that if the Council Tax Base increases relative to the tax base of other councils, then Revenue Support Grant will reduce as a direct consequence.

findings.headline: In-year Council Tax collection rates have declined in recent years due to cost-of-living crisis, despite maintaining 98.5% ultimate collection assumption
findings.detail: The council notes that in-year collection rates have fallen 'in the last few years' driven by the cost-of-living crisis and introduction of premiums. They continue to assume 98.5% ultimate collection rate (unchanged since 2016/17), but acknowledge this is now 'achieved over a longer period of time' rather than in-year. This creates a cash flow timing gap between when amounts are due and when they are actually collected.
findings.matters: Lower in-year collection rates directly affect cash flow forecasting and budget management for the financial year, even if eventual collection remains stable.
findings.figures: In-year collection rates have declined; ultimate collection rate assumed at 98.5%
findings.quote: There have been reduced in-year collection rates in the last few years due to the ongoing cost-of-living crisis and the introduction of premiums. The analysis of the collection rates over recent years indicates that the 98.5% ultimate collection rate is still being achieved, albeit over a longer period of time.

findings.headline: Council must decide by end-March 2026 to implement levy from April 2027; next opportunity is October 2027
findings.detail: The legislation sets a hard deadline: if the council does not decide by 31 March 2026 to introduce the levy, the next implementation date available would be October 2027, requiring a decision 12 months before that. Missing the March deadline delays income by six months.
findings.matters: Timeline-sensitive decision that affects budget forecasting and cashflow planning for 2027-28 onwards; delay reduces revenue in the year it was planned.
findings.figures: Decision deadline: 31 March 2026; Earliest implementation: 1 April 2027; Next implementation window: October 2027
findings.quote: If it does not meet that date then the next date that a Levy can be introduced would be October 2027, subject to a decision 12 months prior.

findings.headline: Visitor levy VAT treatment unresolved; could reduce estimated £3.5m revenue
findings.detail: The financial implications section notes that HM Treasury and HMRC have not yet decided whether VAT applies to the levy. This decision will affect either the fee charged to visitors or the net income received by the council. The impact on actual revenue is currently unknown and material.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director forecasting council resources needs to know that a headline £3.5m estimate carries material uncertainty; the net income could be significantly lower depending on VAT treatment.
findings.figures: £3.5m estimated annual revenue; VAT treatment pending
findings.quote: There is currently no definitive position agreed on the VAT status, HM Treasury and HMRC will decide if VAT applies. When a decision is known, it will impact either or both the levy fee charge and the amount generated for Cardiff.

news_drafts.headline: Cardiff Council faces four-year £167m budget gap as savings targets slip
news_drafts.lead: Cardiff Council has identified a projected budget gap of £167.1 million over four years starting in 2027/28 as it struggles to deliver the major savings needed to balance its budget. During 2025/26, proposals to fundamentally change services delivered only £2.276 million in savings—76 per cent of target—while efficiency-focused savings achieved 88 per cent. The gap reflects sustained demand in social care and children's services, particularly support for children with additional learning needs and specialist school placements. The council's Governance and Audit Committee noted that while the overall 2025/26 financial position was balanced, some directorates recorded significant overspends requiring better control.

news_drafts.headline: Cardiff faces £164m budget gap as funding squeeze collides with care and school cost pressures
news_drafts.lead: Cardiff Council is forecasting a £164m budget gap over four years, with only £119m of the required savings identified so far, the Cabinet was told on 17 September. The gap reflects £224m in cost pressures — driven by long-term care demand and special educational needs — against just £60m in expected funding increases. The council is betting on £45m from council tax rises and efficiency savings, but the scale of the challenge is stark: each 1% shortfall in Welsh Government funding would leave a further £7.2m hole. The council holds reserves at the lower end of adequacy for its size and is already using earmarked money to cover projected school deficits of £9.6m by March 2027. The plan assumes no new details on funding until the Welsh Government's draft budget on 17 November, leaving councillors to build a four-year strategy against a blank page.

news_drafts.headline: Cardiff Council faces £164m budget gap, with £119m in savings unidentified
news_drafts.lead: Cardiff Council faces a £164 million budget gap over four years to 2031, with £119 million in savings still unidentified. Costs are projected to rise by £224 million while funding is expected to increase by only £60 million. Council tax rises of 4.95 per cent a year are assumed to contribute £45 million towards bridging the gap. The council has not yet received its funding settlement from Welsh Government; each one per cent variance from the assumed two per cent annual grant increase would require an additional £7.2 million in savings. The plan acknowledges scenarios ranging from a £17 million gap (if growth is high and inflation low) to £290 million (if funding stays flat and inflation is high).
